soil-found-090.title: Soil science: one resource, many disciplines
soil-found-090.text: Engineers, agronomists, chemists, geologists, ecologists, microbiologists, archaeologists and planners all add to what is known about soils. Soil science gathers that knowledge into the study of soil as a natural resource. It asks how soil forms and how it is classified and mapped. It measures soil's physical, chemical, biological and fertility properties, and asks how they bear on its use and management. The field has two main historical branches. {{ref:soil-found-095}} studies soil in its natural setting. {{ref:soil-found-097}} studies soil in relation to the uses that depend on it. Both draw on the physics, chemistry and biology of soil. Soil occupies {{ref:soil-found-084}}, one of the spheres the geosciences use to organize the Earth. Climate change, greenhouse gases and {{ref:soil-env-212}} now drive much new research, along with interest in biodiversity and in past cultures. Soil scientists also worry about preserving soil and farmland as population and food consumption grow and more land is degraded. Mapping, which classifies the soils of an area and geo-encodes them, increasingly relies on digital methods and remote sensing. In 1998 a new international system, {{ref:soil-class-016}}, replaced the older one from the FAO. Its current 4th edition dates from 2022.

soil-found-078.title: Half solid, half empty: what a soil is made of
soil-found-078.text: Half of a typical soil is not solid at all. About 50% of its volume is solids, 45% mineral grains and 5% material from living things, alive or dead. The other 50% is pores, half filled with water and half with gas. Soil composition describes these proportions. In the short term the mineral and organic shares stay constant, while water and gas trade places. A rise in one is balanced by a fall in the other. Pore space matters because air and water must enter and move through it, and both are critical for soil life. Squeezing a soil, especially under heavy machinery, shrinks its pores and keeps air and water from roots and organisms. Mineral particles, interacting with the organic share, water and gases, clump together into crumbs. Where these crumbs can be identified, the soil is said to be developed. Most nutrients are held by the finest particles of clay and organic material. They cling to clay surfaces, sit bound inside {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, or are locked in living organisms and in long-decayed organic remains. Apart from nitrogen fixed from the atmosphere, most plant nutrients first came from the minerals of the rock or sediment the soil formed from. Living things shape a soil most strongly near the surface. With depth, geochemical influences take over.

soil-found-082.title: Mending poor soils with clay, sand and char
soil-found-082.text: In Thai field trials, a single dose of clay raised yields on low-clay soils by an average of 73%. The trials added a swelling clay once, at 200 kilograms per rai, or 1,300 kg/ha. Soil reclamation improves degraded or badly balanced soils by adding materials such as clay, gypsum, sand, plant and animal remains or {{ref:soil-fert-050}}. Soils too high in clay or salts can be balanced with gypsum and washed river sand. Sandy, nutrient-poor soils benefit from compost or ramial chipped wood. Charred material, modeled on the fertile Amazonian soils covered in {{ref:soil-class-057}}, is used to improve nutrient-poor tropical soils. Uncontrolled use of charred wastes, though, may endanger soil life and human health.

soil-found-081.title: From food to foundations: how people use soil
soil-found-081.text: Soil resources produce 98.8% of the food humans consume. In farming, soil anchors plants and is their primary nutrient base. The kind of soil and the moisture available decide which plants can be grown. Yet soil is not strictly essential. Systems that grow plants in water or mist, with no soil at all, show as much. Soil is also the foundation for most construction and the basis of many building materials. Surface mining, road building and dam construction move massive volumes of it. Waste treatment relies on soil too. Septic systems, covered in {{ref:soil-env-195}}, and wastewater spread on land use soil processes that need oxygen, and landfills use soil as daily cover. Water percolating down to become groundwater is filtered on the way, losing pesticides, hydrocarbons, heavy metals and excess nutrients. Organic soils are a significant fuel and horticultural resource, and drained peatlands are farmed in Nordic countries. Animals and humans even eat soil-like substances, a habit called geophagy. Some monkeys eat soil with their leaves to ease tannin toxicity.

soil-found-085.title: Lichens, microbes and the first bite into bare rock
soil-found-085.text: Bare rock starts becoming soil when living things attack it with acid. The first colonizers, such as lichens, mosses and microbes, begin the work. Lichens and other microorganisms, including cyanobacteria, green algae, fungi and bacteria, secrete oxalic acid. Lichens have long been seen as the pioneers of soil. Seed-bearing plants can colonize faster, but lichens tolerate harsher conditions and dominate in alpine regions. Organic acids from roots and decay, such as citric, phenolic and humic acids and {{ref:soil-chem-060}}, speed chemical breakdown by gripping metal atoms and pulling them from minerals. As the soil thickens, earthworms, burrowing mammals and large animals above ground go on altering its chemistry and fertility.

soil-found-029.title: Minerals, the crystals that build rock and soil
soil-found-029.text: As of August 2026, the International Mineralogical Association recognized 6,228 official mineral species. A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure. That last condition matters. Opal and obsidian are natural solids with no definite crystal structure, so they are more properly called mineraloids. Structure can even split one compound in two. Quartz and stishovite are both silicon dioxide, yet they count as two species. A mineral must also form by natural geological processes. That rule excludes purely human-made products, and biological ones such as seashells. A rock is something else: a bulk solid geologic material made of one mineral or an aggregate of several. Mineralogists classify minerals by their key chemical constituents, chiefly in the Dana and Strunz systems. One family dominates. The minerals described in {{ref:soil-found-031}} make up approximately 90% of the Earth's crust. In soil, minerals form the gritty bulk. The sand and silt fractions are mostly inert rock particles such as quartz, calcite, feldspar and {{ref:soil-chem-135}}.

soil-found-063.title: Lichens, roots and microbes that wear down rock
soil-found-063.text: Two common minerals, albite and muscovite, weather twice as fast in live soil as in sterile soil. Living things make the difference. Biological weathering is weathering started or sped up by soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots. Soil organisms make up about 10 mg/cm3 of typical soils. Lichens are among the most effective agents. In a New Jersey study, hornblende granite under lichen weathered three to four times faster than bare rock. Most commonly, plants release carbon dioxide along with chelating compounds, chemicals that grip metal ions, such as organic acids and {{ref:soil-bio-192}}. Roots can raise carbon dioxide to 30% of all soil gases. The chelating acids strip metal ions, especially aluminum and silicon, from rock. Where they build up, they can reshape whole soils. Partnerships help too. Root-dwelling fungi free nutrients from minerals such as apatite or biotite and pass them to trees, and some bacteria weather minerals in ways that promote plant growth. Life also works by force. Seedlings and roots growing in crevices push rock apart, and lichens pluck mineral grains loose with their hyphae, their thread-like filaments.

soil-found-054.title: Frost weathering and the ice that splits rock
soil-found-054.text: Water expands 9.2% when it freezes. Inside rock, the pressure this creates has a realistic upper limit of 14 megapascals, far above granite's tensile strength of about 4 megapascals. Frost weathering is physical weathering caused by ice forming inside rock outcrops. Frost wedging, the classic explanation, was long believed the main mechanism. It needs small, twisting cracks in almost saturated rock and daily freeze–thaw cycles. Those conditions are unusual, so it is unlikely to matter in the tropics, polar regions or arid climates. Growing theoretical and experimental work now favors ice segregation instead, though the question is still open. Water drawn to the growing ice layers covered in {{ref:soil-phys-154}} can exert up to ten times the pressure of frost wedging. Ice segregation works best between −4 and −15 °C.

soil-found-048.title: What fallen leaves and roots are made of
soil-found-048.text: Fresh plant debris is mostly water, 60% to 90% of it. Dry it, and carbon, oxygen and hydrogen make up about 92% of the weight. The rest includes nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur, calcium, magnesium and trace nutrients. Its organic compounds range from simple sugars to cellulose, along with fats, nitrogen-bearing proteins and, from older woody parts, {{ref:soil-bio-116}}. This debris is the raw material of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. One leftover stands apart. Charcoal, the elemental carbon left by incomplete burning, is highly resistant to decomposition.

soil-found-057.title: Salt weathering: crystals that pry rock apart
soil-found-057.text: Salt can split stone. In salt weathering, also called haloclasty, salty water seeps into cracks and evaporates, leaving salt crystals that grow there. Like {{ref:soil-phys-154}}, the grains draw in more dissolved salt through tiny gaps. They grow into lenses that press hard on the surrounding rock. Sodium and magnesium salts work best. Salt weathering happens wherever evaporation concentrates salts, so it is most common in arid climates and along coasts. In sedimentary rock, weathering of {{ref:soil-chem-134}} to iron(II) sulfate and gypsum can grow salt lenses too.

soil-found-040.title: Clay, the finest and busiest part of soil
soil-found-040.text: Some of the earliest pottery shards date to around 14,000 BCE, which makes clay the longest-known ceramic raw material. Clay is a fine-grained natural soil material containing {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, the hydrous aluminum sheet silicates described in {{ref:soil-found-033}}. In pure form these minerals are mostly white or pale. Impurities color natural clays, and small amounts of iron oxide give red or brown tones. Wet clay is plastic, and firing hardens it. In a field, clay is a mixed blessing. Clay soils drain poorly, which makes them generally less suited to crops. Yet they are more fertile, because they hold on to more positively charged nutrients. Soils rich in swelling clays, which expand as they absorb water, are a major challenge in civil engineering. Mix sand, silt and less than 40% clay, and the result is {{ref:soil-phys-012}}. Clay lasts in rock as well. Shale, formed largely from clay, is the most common sedimentary rock.

soil-found-037.title: The handful of minerals that build most rock
soil-found-037.text: Thousands of mineral species exist, but a few do most of the building. Rock-forming minerals are the species and groups far more abundant in rocks than the rest. The main ones are quartz, the feldspars, {{ref:soil-chem-135}}, amphiboles, pyroxenes, olivines and calcite. All but calcite are silicates. A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals or mineraloids. Some rocks are mostly one mineral: limestone is calcite and quartzite is quartz. Others, like granite, are defined by the proportions of key minerals. Rocks need not be mineral at all. Coal is a sedimentary rock made mainly of organically derived carbon.

soil-found-033.title: Phyllosilicates: minerals built in stacked sheets
soil-found-033.text: Some minerals split into thin, flexible flakes. These are the phyllosilicates, or sheet silicates, made of sheets of linked silica tetrahedra. The class includes {{ref:soil-chem-135}} and the minerals at the heart of {{ref:soil-found-040}}. Each tetrahedron is bound to its neighbors at three oxygen sites, giving a silicon to oxygen ratio of 2:5. That leaves the tetrahedral sheet negatively charged, and a sheet of octahedra balances it. These tetrahedral (T) and octahedral (O) sheets stack into layers, and the stacking defines the groups. In 1:1 minerals, T-O stacks are held together by hydrogen bonds. In 2:1 minerals, T-O-T stacks are held by weaker van der Waals forces. This peeling mineral is also a T-O-T stack, with a difference. It puts aluminum in the tetrahedral sheets, whereas the 1:1 and 2:1 minerals hold Al3+ in the octahedral sites. Metal ions bond its layers together, making them harder. Because the bonds between layers are weak, phyllosilicates show a prominent basal cleavage, a tendency to split along flat planes. Octahedral sheets come in two kinds. When every site is filled they are trioctahedral. When some sites are empty, as in pyrophyllite, they are dioctahedral.

soil-found-041.title: How rain and time turn feldspar into clay
soil-found-041.text: Granite carries the makings of clay. Its orthoclase feldspar weathers to {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and silicic acid, releasing potassium ions. Clay formation is the making of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, most commonly by long chemical weathering of silicate-bearing rocks, and their gathering into deposits. The work is done largely by acid hydrolysis. Weak carbonic acid in rainwater, or acid released by plant roots, breaks the bonds between aluminum and oxygen. Other metal ions and silica come loose, the silica as a gel of orthosilicic acid. Source rock and climate decide the product. Feldspar-rich rock gives kaolin under warm, acid weathering, and {{ref:soil-chem-094}} under alkaline conditions. Igneous rock under alkaline conditions yields {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Intense weathering of other such minerals produces an aluminum hydroxide. Hydrothermal activity can also make them locally. Then the clay may travel. Primary clays stay where they formed, as residual soil deposits. Secondary clays are carried off by flowing water and laid down elsewhere, often in large lakes or marine basins.

soil-found-042.title: Kaolinite, smectite, illite: the main kinds of clay
soil-found-042.text: There are about 30 types of pure clay, but nature rarely serves one alone. Most natural deposits mix several of them with other weathered minerals. The main kinds of clay are grouped by their dominant {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, each with its own entry later: {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, {{ref:soil-chem-093}} and {{ref:soil-chem-094}}. A few others, among them talc and pyrophyllite, are sometimes also classed among them. Chemical and physical tests struggle to tell them apart. X-ray diffraction identifies them most easily. One clay keeps a calendar. Varved clay shows visible annual layers laid down seasonally, and is common in former glacial lakes.

soil-found-064.title: From granite and basalt to soil: weathering's ledger
soil-found-064.text: Turning rock into soil takes between 100 and 1,000 years, a brief interval in geologic time. In that span, weathering turns the minerals of rock into {{ref:soil-chem-079}} and iron oxides. Granite shows the sequence. Hornblende goes first. Biotite then alters to another sheet mineral, and oligoclase and microcline go last. All end as clay and iron oxides. The chemistry shifts with them. Compared with the bedrock, soil from granite loses calcium, sodium and ferrous iron, 40% of its magnesium and 15% of its silicon. It gains at least 50% in aluminum and potassium, triples its titanium and raises its ferric iron by an order of magnitude. Basalt weathers more easily than granite. It formed hotter and drier, and it is fine-grained and glassy. It turns to potassium-poor {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, then to {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. Climate writes the ending. Continuous intense washing by rain, as in rain forests, ends in the aluminum ore of {{ref:soil-chem-108}}. Intense but seasonal monsoon rain ends in an iron- and titanium-rich material, {{ref:soil-form-065}}. Geologists track the progress with the chemical index of alteration, 100 Al2O3/(Al2O3 + CaO + Na2O + K2O). It runs from 47 for unweathered upper crust rock to 100 for fully weathered material.

soil-found-001.title: Soil horizons, the layers that record a soil's life
soil-found-001.text: Cut down through a soil and you usually cross a series of bands. Each band is a horizon: a layer roughly parallel to the surface whose physical, chemical and biological traits differ from those above and below. Horizons are made by soil-forming processes. Layers those processes have not touched are simply called layers. Given time, an undifferentiated soil evolves a profile of two or more horizons. They differ greatly in thickness and generally lack sharp boundaries. Most are recognized by color and texture, described outright or relative to their neighbors, as coarser, sandier or darker. No profile has every major horizon, and some soils, such as soils described in {{ref:soil-class-094}}, have one horizon or none at all. Horizons are also fragile. Erosion can strip the upper ones and bury others downslope, and tillage, tree growth and major earthworks disturb or erase them. Going down a profile goes back in time. Pollen, {{ref:soil-bio-195}} and plant remains record past environmental change, and charcoal allows radiocarbon dating of a horizon. Most classification systems define soil types by horizons, either as whole sequences, as in the German system, or as selected diagnostic horizons. A shorthand of letters and numbers labels each one, recording color, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules.

soil-found-002.title: O, A, E, B, C, R: the alphabet of a soil profile
soil-found-002.text: Six capital letters, most commonly O, A, E, B, C and R, name the main layers of a soil profile. These are the master horizons. Many soils start with an organic surface layer, O. The mineral soil usually begins with an A horizon, the layer with the most organic matter and soil life. Below may lie an E horizon, a leached layer. A B horizon is a well-developed subsoil where substances moving down from the topsoil accumulate. A C horizon is loose but poorly developed material beneath. R is hard bedrock that cannot be dug by hand. Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, and the A and B together normally make up the part described in {{ref:soil-form-024}}. Suffixes of lowercase letters and figures split the master horizons further. Most systems define more horizons and layers than these, and the letters may differ. The USDA field book adds L for limnic, or lake-laid, materials, W for water and M for root-limiting manufactured layers. Because the systems define their symbols differently, they cannot be mixed, and none is more correct than another.

soil-found-020.title: How pH decides which nutrients plants can reach
soil-found-020.text: A soil can be full of nutrients and still starve a crop. Soil pH governs which ions are released or held, and so which nutrients plants can take up. Most minerals dissolve more readily in acid soils. Yet, trading toxicity against need, most nutrients are best available at moderate pH. Below pH 5.0, roots damaged by aluminum take up less, and deficiencies of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium are frequent. Raising pH works unevenly. Molybdenum becomes more available, while zinc, iron, copper and manganese become less so. At high pH these trace nutrients move poorly, a deficit that water-soluble chelates, compounds that hold a metal in soluble form, can correct. Phosphorus was long thought most available near neutrality, at pH 6.5–7.5. Between pH 5.5 and 6.5, though, raising pH may increase, decrease or not affect it. In soils above 2% calcium carbonate, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-035}}, supplying phosphorus, iron, manganese, copper or zinc is often more efficient than trying to acidify.

soil-found-022.title: Soil life and pH, each shaping the other
soil-found-022.text: pH shapes soil life, and soil life shapes pH. Microbes and animals respond to pH directly and through nutrient status, metal toxicity and the forms described in {{ref:soil-bio-095}}, so communities shift as pH changes. At low pH, aluminum causes oxidative stress that harms soft-bodied fauna without a hard outer skeleton: protists, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, {{ref:soil-bio-087}} and earthworms. The traffic runs both ways. Many fungi acidify soil by excreting oxalic acid, which locks calcium into insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Earthworm mucus, weakly alkaline at pH 7.5 to 8, buffers pH. Burrowing animals that mix organic and mineral matter reduce acidity, as in {{ref:soil-bio-096}}.

soil-form-098.title: Asteroid regolith, soil-like dust on tiny worlds
soil-form-098.text: Asteroids wear loose blankets too. Asteroid regolith is the loose surface layer of an asteroid, produced by impacts and other processes that alter its surface. Spacecraft show it ranging from fine-grained deposits to coarse, boulder-rich debris. The Hayabusa mission's samples from Itokawa were the first asteroid regolith grains studied in a laboratory. They showed {{ref:soil-hist-079}} and particles implanted by the solar wind. Hayabusa2 returned samples from Ryugu in 2020, and OSIRIS-REx from Bennu in 2023. Both hold organic- or carbon-rich material and water.

soil-form-087.title: Parent material, the stuff every soil grows from
soil-form-087.text: Every soil carries a family likeness to the material it grew from. Rock is the source of all soil minerals and of every plant nutrient except nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon. Parent material is the underlying geological material in which soil horizons form, generally bedrock or a superficial (drift) deposit. It may be igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock. For a metamorphic rock, the original rock before it changed is the protolith. It may also be loose glacial, river or volcanic deposits. Typical parent minerals include quartz, calcite, feldspar and biotite, one of the minerals covered in {{ref:soil-chem-135}}. The parent leaves a clear mark. Mudstone or shale give clay-rich soils, while sandstone weathers into sandy soils. Parent material also strongly shapes how many basic ions a soil contains. Weatherable minerals in the parent rock favor one kind of {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, called mull, while a shortage of them goes with another, called moder. Soil scientists sort parent materials by how they were deposited. Residual material weathered in place. Transported material was carried by water, wind, ice or gravity. Cumulose material is organic matter that accumulated where it formed. Because soils inherit so much of their structure and minerals from their parent, they are often classified by whether it is consolidated and how it was last transported.

soil-form-106.title: Loess, the wind-blown silt that buries whole regions
soil-form-106.text: Ten percent of Earth's land lies under loess or similar deposits. Loess is a clastic sediment, built of fragments, that is mostly silt-sized and formed by the build-up of wind-blown dust. It holds 20% or less clay, with roughly equal parts sand and silt, typically 20 to 50 micrometres across. Calcium carbonate often cements it loosely. It is even-textured, porous, crumbly, pale yellow or buff and usually unlayered. Its angular grains of quartz, feldspar and {{ref:soil-chem-135}} let it stand in vertical banks. In parts of China people dig cave dwellings into them. Deposits exceed a hundred metres in north-western China, reaching 350 m on the {{ref:soil-form-110}}, and run tens of metres thick in the US Midwest. Pye in 1995 listed four requirements: a dust source, enough wind to carry it, a place to accumulate, and time. Von Leonhard described Löss along the Rhine in 1823–1824, and Lyell popularized the term in 1834. Its wind-blown origin was recognized later, notably by von Richthofen in China in 1878.

soil-form-111.title: Loess–paleosol sequences, climate diaries in silt
soil-form-111.text: Some loess cliffs read like a climate diary. Their stacked layers of loess, separated by buried soils, the {{ref:soil-form-072}}, form layered sequences studied as archives of past climate and environmental change. In China a strong north-west winter monsoon laid down the loess layers. The buried soils record a moist south-east monsoon. Without robust numerical dating, even the place of the last interglacial soil in Austrian and Hungarian loess was long debated. Since the 1980s, luminescence methods have dated when grains last saw daylight. SAR protocols give last-glacial ages accurate to between 5 and 10%. Radiocarbon dating gives reliable ages for the last 40–45 ka, or thousand years, when charcoal or snail shells lie in place.

soil-form-096.title: Volcanic ash, a fast-weathering parent material
soil-form-096.text: Volcanic ash is made largely of glass, and it weathers fast. Ash carried by the wind and settled at various distances from a volcano is called tephra, the most common volcanic parent material. Volcanic ash and lava flows interbedded with loose material are part of Earth's regolith. Soils of siliceous ash consist of glass bubbles and shards with a high internal surface area. They weather rapidly to the clays {{ref:soil-chem-098}} and {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. These soils, classed as {{ref:soil-class-092}}, are highly fertile, rich in organic matter and particularly light for their volume. Volcanic ash is also a source of non-glacial loess, as in Ecuador and Argentina.

soil-form-033.title: Eluviation: how percolating water empties the upper soil
soil-form-033.text: Where more rain falls than evaporates, water keeps moving down through the soil, and it takes things with it. That removal of soil material from upper layers by percolating water is eluviation. It carries mineral and organic colloids, particles fine enough to stay suspended in water. That sets it apart from {{ref:soil-form-050}}, a distinct soil-building mechanism. Acid conditions speed it up, because organic acids make iron and aluminum more soluble. {{ref:soil-form-061}} is the extreme case, stripping out the oxides of iron and aluminum. The layer that loses material is an eluvial horizon. It may be a light-colored zone at the base of the surface mineral horizon, labelled Ae. Where the process is most intense, it forms a separate layer beneath, lettered E and described in {{ref:soil-form-009}}. Some sources count both of these layers as the eluvial zone. What leaves must land somewhere. The material builds up lower down as an illuvial deposit, the process of {{ref:soil-form-032}}. On a slope the exchange also runs downhill: upper facets lose salts while lower facets gain them.

soil-form-023.title: Subsoil, where the rain drops its cargo
soil-form-023.text: Rain does more than wet the ground. It carries weathering products such as clay and iron oxides downward, dissolved or as fine suspended particles, and most of them settle in the subsoil. Subsoil is the layer beneath {{ref:soil-form-021}}, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less soil organic matter. With so little of it, the subsoil's color comes mainly from iron oxides. Physical, chemical and biological activity cluster its particles into a definite arrangement, and that sets it apart from the barely altered substratum below. It is not sterile, but it holds few soil organisms compared with the rich layer above. Most soil mapping systems give it the letter B, with a substratum lettered C beneath; {{ref:soil-form-010}} and {{ref:soil-form-011}} return to both. Human activity has mixed topsoil and subsoil in many environments. Builders have used clay-rich subsoil for millennia, as adobe, cob, rammed earth and wattle and daub.

soil-form-008.title: The A horizon, where life and minerals mix
soil-form-008.text: Earthworms, potworms, arthropods, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, fungi, bacteria and archaea crowd around plant roots in the A horizon, which is why some call it the biomantle. It is the uppermost mineral horizon, at the surface or below an O horizon, where humified soil organic matter is intimately mixed with mineral material. Often called topsoil, it holds dark, decomposed soil organic matter. Burrowing animals stir it into the mineral matter, a mixing described in {{ref:soil-bio-047}}. The original rock structure is fully or largely gone. Biological activity reaches much deeper, though, so it cannot be the chief test, and A horizons are defined mostly relative to the layers beneath. Layers changed by plowing or pasturing count as A horizons, and the suffix p marks plowed ones. The Australian system divides it into A1, dark and most biologically active, A2, paler, and A3, a transition to the layer below.

soil-form-034.title: Cryoturbation: frost that churns the soil
soil-form-034.text: In the coldest soils, the ground will not keep its layers in order. Cryoturbation, or frost churning, mixes material from different horizons, down to bedrock, through repeated freezing and thawing in soils of {{ref:soil-env-129}}, where the ground below stays frozen. It occurs to some degree in most soils of the {{ref:soil-class-096}} order, a name from the Latin gelare, to freeze. In autumn, freezing forms wedges of ice in the most erodible parts of the parent rock, the subject of {{ref:soil-form-036}}. In summer, the part that thaws, described in {{ref:soil-env-146}}, lets loosened material move both down and up. Moisture moves from the warm surface toward the cold, frozen ground below. It dries the upper soil into a granular structure laced with lenses of ice. Coarse material separates from fine, producing {{ref:soil-phys-163}}. Frost churning is the dominant force in that thawing layer and tends to make it uniform. It is strongest on exposed sites and weak in sheltered valleys. Turbels show it in over one-third of the thawing layer, with distorted boundaries between horizons; Orthels show less. In {{ref:soil-phys-160}}, it can bring base-rich water to the surface, neutralizing acidity and replenishing nutrients.

soil-form-010.title: The B horizon, the soil's collecting zone
soil-form-010.text: Brown or reddish, the B horizon takes its color from iron oxides, because it holds less soil organic matter than the A horizon above. It is a subsurface mineral horizon, formed below a horizon lettered A, E, H or O. Its original rock structure is largely gone, and soil-forming processes have altered or enriched its material. It is commonly called subsoil. Where it gathers material moving down from the A and E horizons, it is also called the illuvial horizon. Its marks include residual oxides or clay, lost carbonates or gypsum, and washed-in clay, iron, aluminum, organic material, carbonates, gypsum or silica. It generally has a structure or consistency that differs from the layers above and below. Gleying alone does not make a B horizon, nor do carbonates cut off from a genetic horizon above. The Australian system splits it into B1, transitional from A, B2, with concentrated clay or oxides, and B3, transitional to the C or D horizon.

soil-form-002.title: The soil profile, a record read from the top down
soil-form-002.text: Going down a soil profile means going back in time. Like layers of sediment, its horizons record past events. A soil profile is a vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface. Formally, it is one face of the three-dimensional block described in {{ref:soil-form-003}}. Soil scientists expose a profile by digging a pit or extracting a core with a hand or hydraulic push tube or an auger. Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, but no profile has all the major horizons. Some soils, such as those of the {{ref:soil-class-094}} order, have only one horizon or none. Young soils on mine waste, moraines, volcanic cones, dunes or alluvial terraces are examples. Wind or running water can strip the upper horizons and bury them downslope, a natural process that {{ref:soil-agri-095}} aggravates. Major earthworks or regular deep plowing can leave a soil almost without distinct horizons. The horizons also hold clues to the past. Pollen, {{ref:soil-bio-195}} and plant remains can reveal changes in climate or land use, and large pieces of charcoal allow radiocarbon dating.

soil-found-068.title: Cutans, the coatings left by moving clay
soil-found-068.text: Soil surfaces keep a record of what water carried past them. Cutans are changes in soil texture or structure at the natural surfaces of particles, pores and clumps, caused by illuviation. They are oriented deposits of any soil component: clay skins, or coatings of silica, iron and aluminum oxides, manganese, organic material or carbonate. Clay skins are also called argillans, and a horizon with enough washed-in clay is the kind named in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. Common and visible in the field, they are focal points of chemical and biological reactions. Reading them, a core skill in soil morphology and the study of ancient soils, shows the degree and nature of soil development.

soil-form-040.title: Pedocals, the carbonate soils of an older scheme
soil-form-040.text: Marbut's classification split soils at its highest level into two groups: pedocals and {{ref:soil-class-042}}, the latter rich in aluminum and iron. Pedocals are soils of semiarid and arid regions, rich in calcium carbonate and low in soil organic matter. They were once a class of the order described in {{ref:soil-class-015}}. Under a thin A horizon, calcite and other soluble minerals that water would normally remove build up in the B horizon. There they form a cemented layer, {{ref:soil-chem-036}}. The term is not used in the current US classification, but it often appears in college geology texts.

soil-form-019.title: Albic horizons, bleached layers below the surface
soil-form-019.text: Bleached and pale, the albic horizon is what remains when soil-forming processes move clay and oxides downward. It is a light-colored subsurface diagnostic horizon in both the WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}}. {{ref:soil-class-099}}, acidic soils common in coniferous and boreal forests, usually have one. In {{ref:soil-class-147}} soils it tongues down into a clay-rich Bt horizon. In {{ref:soil-class-144}}, the topsoil can be completely bleached. {{ref:soil-class-137}} often show eluviation as an albic horizon beneath an umbric surface layer.

soil-form-031.title: Cambic horizons, the first signs of change below ground
soil-form-031.text: The cambic horizon is the diagnostic horizon of last resort. It is a subsurface horizon showing early change by soil-forming processes, recognized when it does not meet the requirements of any other diagnostic horizon. It lacks appreciable illuviated clay, organic carbon, iron and aluminum oxyhydroxides, carbonate, gypsum or soluble salts. Its texture must be no coarser than loamy fine sand or very fine sand. It is commonest in {{ref:soil-class-101}} and {{ref:soil-class-100}}, also occurs in {{ref:soil-class-092}} and is written Bw or Bg. Along a {{ref:soil-form-063}}, it gains clay and develops into a clay-enriched Bt horizon once the soil becomes one of the {{ref:soil-class-090}} kind.

soil-form-018.title: Epipedons, the diagnostic surface horizons of USDA taxonomy
soil-form-018.text: {{ref:soil-class-006}} gives the top of the soil its own set of names. An epipedon is a diagnostic surface horizon, the upper part of the soil. There are eight: the anthropic, folistic, histic, melanic, mollic, ochric, plaggen and umbric epipedons. A fertile mollic epipedon, built by long additions of root-derived organic material, is the defining feature of {{ref:soil-class-101}}. {{ref:soil-class-098}} must have a histic epipedon, while an ochric epipedon is common in {{ref:soil-class-094}} and {{ref:soil-class-093}}. {{ref:soil-class-100}} usually have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon. Plaggen or anthropic epipedons signal intense, prolonged human activity.

soil-form-050.title: Leaching: how water strips a soil from the top down
soil-form-050.text: Water soaking down through a soil does not travel empty. Leaching is the removal of soluble materials from one zone of a soil to another by water moving through the profile. It differs from eluviation, which moves tiny mineral and organic particles, called colloids, rather than dissolved material. Both tend to strip the topsoil and enrich the subsoil, in a horizon called the zone of illuviation. Climate sets the pace directly. Leaching is most intense in warm, humid regions where the soil does not freeze. The red tropical soil described in {{ref:soil-form-065}} develops under high temperatures and heavy rainfall, and intensive leaching leaves it less fertile than other soils. Its signature shows in the profile. In one brownish leached soil, {{ref:soil-class-049}}, water washes mobile chemicals out of the A horizon. Iron and aluminum oxides, the subject of {{ref:soil-form-085}}, gather in the B horizon and color it rusty orange-brown. The Canadian system for naming soils marks strongly leached layers as light gray Ae horizons. In Solonetzic soils, progressive leaching moves salts and sodium downward. The process can also defeat reclamation: intensive leaching has left reclaimed {{ref:soil-chem-030}} infertile.

soil-phys-015.title: One yardstick from clay specks to giant boulders
soil-phys-015.text: The finest clay and the largest boulder sit on a single scale. Engineers following ISO 14688-1 run it from clay at 0.002 mm or less to large boulders over 630 mm. That quantity is grain size: the diameter of individual grains of sediment. It also covers the particles cemented into clastic rocks, which are built from fragments of older rock. A grain is not the same as a crystal. Crystallite size is the size of a single crystal, and one grain can contain several. Above the tiny colloidal particles and clay, ever-coarser classes climb toward cobbles and boulders. The first of them is {{ref:soil-phys-013}}. The Udden-Wentworth scale, used in the United States, sets its named classes by size ranges. With texture and the spread of pore sizes, grain-size data help estimate {{ref:soil-water-193}}, the ease with which water flows through soil. One such rule of thumb is Allen Hazen's, covered in {{ref:soil-water-194}}.

soil-phys-013.title: Silt, the grain at the edge of eyesight
soil-phys-013.text: The unaided eye can just see a grain about 63 microns across. That marks the top of silt, a granular material finer than sand and coarser than clay, mostly broken quartz. Geologists place it at about 4 to 63 microns; the USDA uses 0.05 to 0.002 mm. Near 2 to 4 microns, quartz fragments give way to {{ref:soil-chem-079}}. Dry silt feels floury, and wet silt will not hold a molded shape. Between the teeth it feels gritty, where clay feels smooth. Silt is made by grinding quartz, in dust storms of very hot climates and by glaciers in very cold ones. Wind-laid silt forms loess, some of the most fertile farmland on Earth. Its quartz adds no nutrients but helps soil build excellent structure. Silt erodes easily, has poor mechanical properties and can liquefy in earthquakes. Settling in still water, 60-micron grains fall a meter in five minutes; 2-micron grains take several days.

soil-phys-054.title: Two meanings of clay: a size and a mineral
soil-phys-054.text: The word clay hides two different ideas. One is a class of very fine particle sizes; the other is material made of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}. The two overlap but differ. The size boundary with silt depends on the discipline: 2 μm for soil scientists, 4–5 μm for many sedimentologists, 1 μm for colloid chemists. Geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity rather than size, using {{ref:soil-phys-021}}. A clay-sized grain may be very fine quartz, sharing clay's surface-area traits but not its {{ref:soil-chem-047}}, the holding of nutrients.

soil-phys-053.title: Why wet clay keeps any shape pressed into it
soil-phys-053.text: Press wet clay into a shape, and it stays put. That is plasticity, clay's defining mechanical property: the capacity, when wet, to be molded into a shape it then keeps. It comes from {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, whose thin plates are tough but flexible and cling together when moist. In {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, a film of water molecules holds the plates together through hydrogen bonds. The bond is weak enough to let plates slip during molding, yet strong enough to hold the new shape. Drying removes most of the water, so the plates bond directly and the clay turns rigid but fragile. Wet it again, and it turns plastic. Clay stays plastic only from just moist enough to mold to just dry enough to hold a shape. For this clay, those thresholds sit near 36% to 40% and 58% to 72% water. The dry threshold has its own entry, {{ref:soil-phys-023}}. So does the wet one, {{ref:soil-phys-022}}.

soil-phys-055.title: Heavy, wet and surprisingly fertile: farming on clay
soil-phys-055.text: Clay has a poor reputation on the farm, yet good soil needs some of it. A high clay content trades poor drainage against greater fertility. Clay soils hold water and drain poorly, so they often need artificial drainage and tillage before crops thrive. In return, their higher {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, the power to hold nutrients, makes them more fertile. That keeps more land in production rather than lying fallow. Their tightly bonded particles also resist wind and water erosion better than silty and sandy soils.

soil-phys-040.title: Why texture outranks color in the life of a crop
soil-phys-040.text: A farmer sizing up a field should care more about its grains than its color. The physical properties of soil are its measurable physical traits, and for crops they rank in a clear order. Texture comes first, then structure, {{ref:soil-phys-060}}, porosity, consistency, temperature, color and resistivity. They change with depth through the soil's layers, and most govern aeration and how water enters and stays. Texture is the blend of coarse, medium and fine mineral grains. Coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus bind those grains into larger units, described in {{ref:soil-phys-003}}. Density with pores included, measured at a standard moisture, estimates compaction. Sandy soils drain fast, stay airy and warm quickly in spring, but hold little water and few nutrients. Clay soils store water and nutrients and resist pH change, yet drain very slowly and compact easily. Silty soils sit in between, and wind and rain carry them off easily.

soil-phys-028.title: Clays that heave houses and pull roots apart
soil-phys-028.text: Damage from shrinking and swelling clay soils is estimated at $7 billion a year. Shrink–swell capacity is the degree to which certain {{ref:soil-chem-079}} in a soil expand when wet and contract when dry. The culprits include {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, {{ref:soil-chem-095}} and {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, and more of them means more severe movement. A soil with at least 5 percent of them by weight may shrink and swell. It is measured as the coefficient of linear extensibility, or COLE. A COLE of 0.06 means 100 inches of soil swell by 6 inches, and anything above 0.06 can damage structures. Swelling heaves buildings, and shrinking lets foundations settle unevenly. Damage peaks where wet and dry seasons are sharp. These soils belong to the order covered in {{ref:soil-class-106}}. Drying opens deep cracks that let water reach lower layers, so the cycle repeats. Shrinking can pull crop roots apart, yet the cracks help the soil recover fast from compaction.

soil-phys-001.title: How grains and gaps build a living soil
soil-phys-001.text: A farmer cannot change the mineral grains in a field, but can wreck or rebuild the way they fit together. That arrangement is soil structure: how a soil's solid particles sit, and the pore spaces left between them. Texture is innate, fixed by the mineral particles themselves, the separates described in {{ref:soil-phys-047}}. Structure is not. It depends on how particles clump, bind and gather into aggregates, small crumbs of particles stuck together. Those clumps in turn set the pattern of pores. Through that pattern, structure shapes how water and air move, how heat travels, and how roots and seedlings push through. It also governs biological activity and how well the soil resists erosion. Structure never sits still. Tillage, wheel traffic, roots, microbes and soil animals reshape it, and so do rain, wind, wetting and drying, and freezing and thawing. Most cultivation does harm. Mechanical mixing compacts and shears aggregates, fills pores and exposes organic matter to faster decay. Continued cultivation and traffic can press compacted, impermeable layers called hardpans into the soil profile. Irrigation brings its own damage, as aggregates break apart and clay disperses on rapid wetting. {{ref:soil-chem-009}} suffer most, because sodium makes wet particles push one another apart. Yet the choice and timing of farming practices can improve structure as well as destroy it. Read with care, structure is also a record. It holds clues to a soil's texture, organic matter, biology, history and human use, and to the chemistry under which it formed.

soil-phys-003.title: Peds: the natural building blocks of soil
soil-phys-003.text: A lump of earth gets a different name depending on who made it. When soil-forming processes build it, it is a ped: a natural aggregate of soil particles, set apart from its neighbors by pores or voids. When cultivation makes it, it is merely a clod. The word, a contraction of pedolith, is used mostly for visible units larger than 1 mm seen in the field. Peds form as sand, silt and clay clump into aggregates, and aggregates clump into larger units. Coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus glue them into fairly stable secondary structures. Some soils are structureless, while others have simple units or compound units built of smaller ones. The gaps between peds are one way large pores, or {{ref:soil-water-189}}, form, alongside roots, cracks and soil animals. Peds are best described when soil is dry or slightly moist, because wet peds blur together.

soil-phys-029.title: Expansive clay and the builders who outwit it
soil-phys-029.text: Builders sometimes leave empty space under a slab on purpose. The reason is expansive clay, a clay soil that swells and shrinks greatly as its water content changes. Its minerals have an expanding 2:1 layered lattice, though not every 2:1 clay expands. Lab tests look for high plasticity, a free swell test comparing water and kerosene, or {{ref:soil-chem-093}} under X-rays. Field signs include mounds and hollows, deep cracks, and moist soil that rolls into a 3 mm thread without crumbling. Builders also use piles, lime stabilizers and steady moisture.

soil-phys-048.title: Albert Atterberg draws soil's first size lines
soil-phys-048.text: Soil's size classes began with studies in southern Sweden. In 1905 the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-011}} proposed the first particle-size classification, the international soil texture system. He capped silt at 20 μm for four reasons. Finer particles are invisible and clump together with salts. They also wick water upward fastest over 24 hours and leave pores too small for root hairs. Commission One of the International Society of Soil Science recommended it in 1927. Australia adopted it; its equal logarithmic size steps are seen as worth keeping. The USDA went its own way in 1938.

soil-phys-056.title: Well graded or poorly graded: why the size mix matters
soil-phys-056.text: Poorly graded ground drains better than well-graded ground but liquefies more easily. Soil gradation is an engineering classification of a coarse-grained soil by the range of particle sizes it contains. Gravels and sands with a good spread of sizes, from the No. 4 to the No. 200 sieve, are well graded. The rest are poorly graded, either uniformly graded or gap-graded. Their extra voids explain the drainage, while well-graded soils compact further. Gradation is read from the grain-size curve covered in {{ref:soil-phys-020}}, using the AASHTO system or {{ref:soil-phys-036}}. Fine-grained silts and clays are classed instead by {{ref:soil-phys-021}}.

soil-phys-052.title: Watching grains settle with a beam of X-rays
soil-phys-052.text: Settling soil can be tracked with X-rays as well as with a floating gauge. X-ray sedimentation is a hybrid particle-sizing technique that combines sedimentation with X-ray absorption. Stokes' law turns each particle's terminal settling velocity, its steady sinking speed, into a size, as in {{ref:soil-phys-050}}. The X-rays supply the amounts. Their absorption, read through the Beer–Lambert–Bouguer law, gives the relative mass concentration in each size class. It is one of several further quantitative texture methods, alongside the pipette, {{ref:soil-bio-118}} and rapid methods.

soil-phys-036.title: The Unified Soil Classification System: soil in two letters
soil-phys-036.text: Engineers across North America describe a soil with just two letters. Those letters come from the Unified Soil Classification System, or USCS, which classes soils by texture and grain size. It is the most common engineering classification in North America and works for most unconsolidated materials. The first letter names the main material: G for gravel, S for sand, M for silt, C for clay and O for organic soil. Peat gets PT. The second letter gives grading, W for well graded or P for poorly graded, or {{ref:soil-phys-022}}, H for high and L for low. Soils fall into three major groups: coarse-grained sands and gravels, fine-grained silts and clays, and highly organic soils, or peat. Sieves draw the first line. A soil is coarse-grained if more than 50% stays on the No. 200 sieve, whose openings are 0.075 mm. The No. 4 sieve, with 4.75 mm openings, separates sand from gravel. Under the USCS, silt particles measure 0.002–0.075 mm and sand particles 0.075–4.75 mm. Sands and gravels are then divided by grain size and grading. Silts and clays are divided by their Atterberg limits into high- and low-plasticity soils. With 5–12% fines, the silt and clay particles, both grading and plasticity count. A dual symbol may then appear, such as GW-GM for well-graded gravel with silt. Europe's ISO 14688 is very similar but adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

soil-phys-021.title: Atterberg limits: the water contents where soil changes state
soil-phys-021.text: Add water to a dry fine-grained soil, and it passes from solid to semi-solid to plastic to liquid. The Atterberg limits are the critical water contents that mark where it crosses from one of these states to the next. A Swedish chemist and agronomist, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-011}}, devised them in 1911. He also proposed the first soil particle-size classification, described in {{ref:soil-phys-048}}. Arthur Casagrande, a pioneer of soil mechanics, later refined them. Because the changes are gradual, standard tests fix each boundary by convention. The first of those tests appears in {{ref:soil-phys-022}}. The tests suit clayey and silty soils, which shrink, swell and change strength as their moisture varies. Fine-grained soils are classified mainly by these limits rather than by grain size. The limits are simple to measure and closely tied to compressibility, permeability and strength, so they offer quick estimates of all three.

soil-phys-023.title: Plastic limit: the thread that breaks at 3.2 mm
soil-phys-023.text: A standard soil test needs little more than a rolled thread of soil. The plastic limit is the water content below which a soil turns brittle and can no longer be rolled into a thin thread. Rolled on a flat, non-porous surface, the thread breaks at larger diameters as it dries. The limit is the moisture content, by weight, at which it breaks apart at 3.2 mm, about 1/8 inch. A soil that never reaches 3.2 mm at any moisture is non-plastic. Remolded soil here is quite stiff, near 200 kPa of {{ref:soil-phys-103}}.

soil-phys-026.title: Liquidity index: where a soil's water sits between limits
soil-phys-026.text: Where a soil's natural water content, W, falls between its limits says much about how strong it is once remolded. The liquidity index places W on the scale from plastic to liquid limit: LI = (W − PL)/(LL − PL). At 0 the soil sits at its plastic limit, near 200 kPa of {{ref:soil-phys-103}}. At 1 it sits at its liquid limit, with only about 2 kPa. A companion consistency index, (LL − W)/(LL − PL), runs the other way, and the two always add up to 1.

soil-phys-027.title: Clay activity: same clay content, different behavior
soil-phys-027.text: Two soils with the same amount of clay can behave very differently, because {{ref:soil-chem-079}} differ. Clay activity is the ratio of a soil's plasticity index to its clay-size fraction, used to judge how active its clay is. Below 0.75 the clay is inactive, above 1.25 active, and in between normal. {{ref:soil-chem-093}} has liquid limits of 100–900%, against 60–120% for {{ref:soil-chem-094}} and 30–110% for {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. The ratio links clay as a size to clay as a mineral, the split explained in {{ref:soil-phys-054}}.

soil-phys-024.title: Shrinkage limit: the point where drying clay stops shrinking
soil-phys-024.text: A drying clay shrinks, but only up to a point. The shrinkage limit is the water content below which further drying no longer makes a soil shrink. It is used much less often than the liquid and plastic limits. Its value depends on the kind of clay. Reported shrinkage limits run 8.5–15% for {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, 15–17% for {{ref:soil-chem-094}} and 25–29% for {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. So the last of these clays stops shrinking while it still holds far more water than the first does.

soil-phys-005.title: Soil aggregation: turning loose grains into lasting crumbs
soil-phys-005.text: Earthworms, fungi, frost and chemistry all work on the same project: turning loose grains into crumbs. Soil aggregation is the joining of primary soil particles into larger aggregates through rearrangement, flocculation and cementation. Flocculated clumps become true aggregates only once something cements them. Carbonates, gypsum, clay particles, organic matter and sesquioxides, the oxides of iron and aluminum, all serve as cement. {{ref:soil-bio-050}} and fungal hyphae strengthen the bonds. So do multivalent cations bridging negatively charged particles, and hydrogen and hydrophobic bonds between organic compounds. Calcium bridges clay and organic matter. It can also replace sodium on particle surfaces, curbing the dispersion, crusting and bursting of crumbs that plague {{ref:soil-chem-009}}. The best glue depends on the clay. Organic matter is the main binder with swelling 2:1 clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, met in {{ref:soil-phys-029}}. With oxides and 1:1 clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, electrostatic bonds join in, and aggregation is weaker. Sesquioxides cement aggregates larger than 100 μm, especially in soils with more than 10% sesquioxides. Weather shuffles the pieces. Wetting and drying, and shrinking and swelling, rearrange particles and can either strengthen or weaken aggregates. Freezing wet soil breaks aggregates into smaller ones. Some shrink-swell soils even mulch themselves, building a granular surface through repeated shrinking and swelling. Life builds aggregates too, through earthworm casts, the fecal pellets of mites and collembola, roots and fungal hyphae. These biological agents matter most where swelling 2:1 clays are lacking.

soil-phys-031.title: Soil crust: the hard surface that turns rain away
soil-phys-031.text: When rain will not soak into bare ground, the culprit is usually the surface itself. A soil crust is a surface layer, often hardened and platy, that differs from the soil beneath it. Physical crusts form under the impact of raindrops or trampling. Salts and silica collect in them, so they are often harder than uncrusted soil. They cut infiltration, the soaking of water into soil, hinder plants trying to establish and erode quickly once broken. In arid and semi-arid regions, intense rain soon outpaces a sealed surface, and the excess runs off overland. Better soil structure means less crusting and better seedling emergence. Coarse organic matter left on the surface helps prevent crusts, and on {{ref:soil-chem-009}}, so does calcium swapped for sodium. Other crusts are alive, formed by communities of surface microorganisms, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-032}}.

soil-phys-010.title: Rebuilding the crumb: how farmers repair soil structure
soil-phys-010.text: Each extra millimeter of rain that good structure lets soak in can add 10 kg/ha to a wheat yield. Improving soil structure means practices that push soil toward a granular, crumb structure. They raise porosity, organic matter and the activity of microbes and soil animals. The rewards are less erosion, more water soaking in, easier rooting and fewer crusts blocking seedlings. Mulch, manure and compost, practiced since people first settled to farm, build stable bridges between mineral particles. Where warm, moist climates break down organic matter too fast, charcoal served instead, as in pre-Columbian {{ref:soil-class-053}}. {{ref:soil-fert-050}} is the modern version. Lime helps because divalent calcium bridges negatively charged clay and organic molecules. Advisers urge pasture phases in rotations, less tillage and ground cover against raindrops. On irrigated {{ref:soil-chem-009}}, gypsum lets calcium displace sodium. Less tillage is no cure-all, though: in irrigated horticulture, no-till usually loses productivity as structure degrades.

soil-phys-033.title: Soil dispersion: how sodium makes clay wash away
soil-phys-033.text: A dispersive soil can look perfectly sound until digging lets running water reach it. Soil dispersion is the breakdown of soil, especially sodium-rich clay, into separate fine particles that water easily washes away. It is the opposite of flocculation, and soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content control both. Sodium drives the damage. At high levels, sodium ions break clay platelets apart, so wet particles repel one another and aggregates fall to pieces. Calcium and magnesium do the reverse, promoting flocculation. The key gauge is the {{ref:soil-chem-018}}, sodium's share of all the cations a soil holds. Above 5%, dispersion becomes possible, and above 15% it is highly likely. Dispersive layers usually hide in the subsoil, where clay and sodium concentrate. They feel soapy and often have prismatic or columnar structure. Such soils are commoner in old landscapes, and sodium collects low in the landscape. Once exposed, dispersed soil feeds gully and tunnel erosion, degrades structure and turns water turbid. Where the particles settle, they clog and seal the surface. Irrigation can bring the same collapse, as aggregates break down and clay disperses on rapid wetting. Management is mostly restraint: avoid disturbance, keep vegetation cover and control salt. Where the soil has already been disturbed, gypsum is added.

soil-phys-043.title: Up to 1,000 square meters of surface in a gram
soil-phys-043.text: A single gram of clay typically carries 10 to 1,000 square meters of surface, spread across thin plates. Specific surface area captures this: the surface area of soil particles per unit mass. Sand has the least specific surface area and is the least active, silt sits in the middle, and clay is the most active. Surface matters because of what happens on it. Together with the particles' unbalanced electric charges, it sets their role in fertility, measured as {{ref:soil-chem-046}}. Clay's vast surface and many negative charges let soil hold water and nutrients. Even the water held at {{ref:soil-water-177}}, after excess water drains away, depends on surface area. Surface is not everything, though. Particles of one texture class share traits tied to surface area, such as moisture retention, but not those tied to composition, such as this exchange capacity.

soil-phys-009.title: Slaking: when trapped air bursts soil crumbs
soil-phys-009.text: Drop a dry crumb of soil into water, and the air trapped inside can blow it apart. That is slaking, the break-up of aggregates when entering water displaces air from pores and bursts aggregates holding trapped air. It is purely mechanical, one of the direct ways water destroys soil structure. In the field, slaking follows raindrop impact, so ground cover protects against both. Stable aggregates resist it, along with crusting and erosion. In {{ref:soil-chem-009}}, calcium that replaces sodium on particle surfaces eases slaking, dispersion and crusting alike.

soil-phys-030.title: Gilgai, the lumpy ground that churning clay builds
soil-phys-030.text: In some clay country, the ground rises and dips in a pattern of small mounds and hollows. This is gilgai: a microrelief, or small-scale bumpiness, of alternating mounds and depressions on shrink–swell clay soils. It forms in {{ref:soil-class-106}}, where repeated shrinking and swelling churns the soil and heaves deeper material to the surface. Field surveys treat gilgai, along with deep shrinkage cracks, as a visible sign of expansive soil. One USDA soil-order list applies the name to the deep cracks themselves.

soil-phys-125.title: Seepage: water on the move through soil
soil-phys-125.text: Still water in soil does little harm. Moving water can bring down a levee. Seepage is the movement of water through soil. Below the {{ref:soil-water-247}}, where pore water pressure rises evenly with depth, conditions are hydrostatic and nothing flows. A sloping or perched water surface sets water seeping. The rate follows {{ref:soil-water-201}}. Flow is proportional to how fast excess pressure changes with distance, scaled by how freely the soil passes water and by the fluid's viscosity. The ease of flow varies enormously, from about 10−12 m/s in clays to about 10−1 m/s in gravels. In steady seepage, velocities do not change with time; that does not hold while water levels are changing or the soil is consolidating. Upward seepage lowers effective stress. At the critical {{ref:soil-phys-166}}, it reaches zero, the soil loses nearly all strength, and less permeable layers may heave. This state, also called a boiling condition, is the one behind {{ref:soil-phys-116}} and {{ref:soil-phys-118}}. Strength lost to upward seepage often helps cause levee failures. Fast seepage also drags particles away from where it comes out. The erosion works back upslope as soil piping, which can fail a structure and open sinkholes. To stop seepage below dams, engineers build impermeable curtains of {{ref:soil-chem-100}}, a clay almost fully saturated with sodium.

soil-phys-070.title: Five sizes of soil pore, from cracks to cryptopores
soil-phys-070.text: A pore's size decides what water it holds and what can live in it. A widely used grouping, after Brewer (1964), sorts soil pores by diameter. The largest class, {{ref:soil-water-189}}, are over 75 μm, too large for significant capillary force. Unless closed off, they drain and are usually full of air at the wetness described in {{ref:soil-water-177}}. They form where soil cracks, where peds and aggregates separate, and along roots and burrows. Mesopores, 30–75 μm, are the largest pores still full of water at that point. Called storage pores, they hold water that plants and soil organisms can use, so soil scientists study them closely for agriculture and irrigation. Micropores, 5–30 μm, hold water that is practically immobile yet still available to plants, so dissolved substances move through them mainly by diffusion. Ultramicropores, 0.1–5 μm, shelter microbes inside aggregates from predators such as amoebae and {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, and their volume tracks bacterial biomass. Texture and organic matter set them, and compaction barely touches them. Cryptopores, under 0.1 μm, are too small for most microbes. Organic matter inside them is protected from decay, and their water is barely available to plants.

soil-phys-128.title: Specific storage: water released as pressure falls
soil-phys-128.text: Lower the water pressure in a saturated aquifer and it gives up some of its water. Specific storage is the volume released from a unit volume of aquifer when the water's pressure level falls by one unit. It reflects how compressible both the aquifer and the water are. Storativity, or the storage coefficient, is the same release per unit area of aquifer. For a confined aquifer it is specific storage summed over the thickness. In an unconfined aquifer storativity roughly equals the {{ref:soil-phys-129}}, because release from specific storage is orders of magnitude smaller.

soil-phys-091.title: Preventing compaction, since cures take decades
soil-phys-091.text: Partly restoring a compacted soil takes several decades, so prevention matters most. Controlled traffic keeps wheel tracks apart from rooting areas, and low tyre pressure spreads a machine's load over a larger surface. Models of field vulnerability help farmers avoid driving on susceptible soil. Where damage is done, deep ripping can loosen compacted layers. Biology helps too. Deep-rooting crops break impermeable layers, add organic matter and drive wetting and drying cycles that crack the soil. Growing crops and trees on the same site, as {{ref:soil-agri-140}}, regenerates compacted soil over the long run. The planting pits described in {{ref:soil-agri-057}}, 20–40 cm across and 10–20 cm deep, are filled with organic matter, capture water and gradually rehabilitate the soil beneath. Adding lime raises pH to suit microbes and earthworms, whose activity loosens the soil. The EU's Seventh Environment Action Programme, in force from 2014, addresses compaction, and a German federal soil law obliges farmers to guard against it.

soil-water-180.title: How rain soaks into the ground, and when it stops
soil-water-180.text: Sand and well-aggregated soils can take in 2.5 cm of rain an hour, while high-clay soils accept as little as 0.25 cm. That intake is infiltration, the process by which water on the ground surface enters the soil. Gravity drives it, helped by capillary forces, absorption and osmosis. Infiltration capacity is the maximum rate, usually given in meters per day. It lasts only while there is room at the surface, which depends on porosity and on how fast earlier water moves down through the {{ref:soil-phys-069}}. As a storm goes on, that room shrinks. Infiltrated water fills storage and weakens capillary pull. Wetted clays swell and narrow their pores. Raindrops striking bare ground wash fine particles into surface pores. Robert E. Horton suggested that capacity drops quickly early in a storm, then settles to a near-constant value after a couple of hours. When rain arrives faster than the soil can take it in, the surplus usually runs off, unless a physical barrier holds it in place. Rates are measured in the field with devices such as {{ref:soil-water-187}}, permeameters and {{ref:soil-water-256}}.

soil-water-193.title: Hydraulic conductivity, the measure of how fast water moves
soil-water-193.text: A well sunk into sand and gravel draws water far more easily than one in clay or unfractured granite. The difference is hydraulic conductivity, written K: how easily water moves through a material's pores or fractures, in meters per second. K depends on the material's intrinsic {{ref:soil-water-191}}, on how saturated it is, and on the density and viscosity of the fluid. Formally, it is the ratio of volume flux to {{ref:soil-phys-166}}, the flow per unit area divided by the slope that drives it. Saturated hydraulic conductivity, Ksat, describes flow through saturated material. Natural values span many orders of magnitude, often in a lognormal pattern, and vary greatly from place to place. Direction matters: vertical K can be orders of magnitude below horizontal K. So does scale, since testing a cubic meter of an aquifer, a water-bearing layer, generally gives a different answer from a cubic centimeter sample. In unsaturated soil, K depends non-linearly on {{ref:soil-water-164}}. One material's unsaturated K spans a wider range than saturated K does across all materials. K is estimated from grain-size and pore-size distributions and texture, or measured in laboratory and field tests interpreted with {{ref:soil-water-201}}.

soil-water-201.title: Darcy's law, born in the sand filters of Dijon
soil-water-201.text: From the 1830s the engineer Henry Darcy studied water flowing through sand filters, hoping to improve the water supply of Dijon, France. In 1856 he published the result in a construction report. Darcy's law is an equation describing the flow of a fluid through a porous medium, and it became the basis of hydrogeology. Like Ohm's law for electricity, it makes flow rate proportional to a difference, here in {{ref:soil-phys-165}}. Hydraulic conductivity plays the part of electrical conductivity. Flow rises with the medium's permeability, its cross-section and the pressure drop. It falls with the fluid's viscosity and the length of the path. Without a pressure gradient nothing flows. The Darcy flux is a flow per unit area, not the speed of water in the pores; porosity links the two. The law holds only for slow, smooth, laminar flow, as in most groundwater, at Reynolds numbers below one, and up to 10 in tests. Very coarse sediments may flow turbulently and escape it.

soil-water-247.title: The water table, where saturated ground begins
soil-water-247.text: In the Nile Delta, wheat tolerates a water table 45 cm below the surface, while cotton needs 90 cm. The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturation. Below it, pores and fractures are full of groundwater; above it lies the unsaturated zone. It sits where water pressure equals atmospheric pressure. In soils with strong capillarity, water is drawn up above it in a damp band. The level rises and falls with rain and with water lost by evaporation and plants. In Britain or California it is lower in summer, and the band between levels is the zone of intermittent saturation. It is rarely flat. Its slope, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-166}}, depends on recharge, withdrawal and permeability. Where it meets the surface, springs, rivers and lakes appear, and groundwater inflow sustains their base flow. A perched water table sits above the regional one, on an impermeable or slowly permeable layer. A well in a confined aquifer shows a potentiometric surface instead.

soil-water-181.title: Why litter, cracks and roots speed water into soil
soil-water-181.text: On sandy loam, infiltration under leaf litter can be nine times that of bare ground. Bare soil forms a crust or surface seal that keeps it low. Rainfall, soil and surface conditions together control how fast water enters a soil. Rain infiltrates faster than snow or sleet. Entry is rapid early in a storm, while the soil is unsaturated, and slows as it saturates. Dry soils have the highest capacity, partly saturated soils a moderate one, and saturated soils no room for more. Fine-pored clays take water more slowly than coarse sands, except dry clays, which crack and take it quickly. Compaction lowers porosity and so capacity. After wildfires, water-repellent soils can cut infiltration sharply or stop it. Roots and burrowing animals open cracks that speed it. With no vegetation, rates can be very low, causing excess runoff and erosion. Pavement prevents infiltration, and steeper slopes shed water faster. {{ref:soil-chem-019}} have poor structure, so rainwater ponds and evaporates before crops can use it.

soil-water-222.title: Soil moisture sensors and the sprinkler that knows better
soil-water-222.text: Wired to an irrigation clock, a soil moisture sensor makes a smart controller that skips watering when the soil is already wet. The sensor estimates the volumetric water content of soil, usually indirectly. Instead of drying and weighing a sample, it reads a proxy such as electrical resistance, dielectric constant or interaction with neutrons. The link between proxy and moisture must be calibrated, and it can shift with the kind of soil, its temperature and electrical conductivity. Technologies include frequency domain reflectometry, capacitance sensors, time domain reflectometry and transmission, neutron gauges, soil resistivity and galvanic cells. Capacitance sensors resemble the sensors covered in {{ref:soil-water-226}}. But where those work at several hundred MHz, capacitance sensors run below 1 MHz and pick up more noise. A separate class of sensors, such as {{ref:soil-water-221}} and gypsum blocks, measures water potential instead of content. Farmers use sensors to irrigate with less water, raising yield and quality through better moisture control at critical growth stages.

soil-water-215.title: Draining farmland, from Dutch steam pumps to Florida citrus
soil-water-215.text: In the Netherlands, 15th-century windpumps could drain only marginal land. The Haarlemmermeer had to wait for large steam pumps, which drained it between 1849 and 1852. Agricultural land drainage removes excess water from farmland, from wetland soils to fields waterlogged for short spells, so that crops are not damaged. Clay-rich soils pass water down very slowly, and hardpans or shallow rock block it. When excess water shuts out air, roots suffocate. Even excellent soils waterlogged for a week of the year can lose their fruit trees. Ditches turned glacial marshes in the northern United States and Europe into mucklands for vegetables and other high-value crops. Florida's flatwoods citrus groves are pumped after heavy rain. Rice needs complete water control, since fields are flooded or drained at different stages. Evapotranspiration concentrates the salts in irrigation water, so irrigated land may need periodic over-irrigation and drainage. {{ref:soil-chem-030}} are an exception: subsurface drainage is normally not advisable, though surface drainage in rainy periods can help reclaim them.

soil-water-216.title: Fabric filters that keep drains from clogging
soil-water-216.text: Drain filters of the kind covered in {{ref:soil-water-254}} are synthetic fabrics that hold back fine soil particles but let water through, so a drain does not clog. In a typical drain the fabric lines a trench filled with gravel, shells or stone. It is folded over the top and covered with soil, and groundwater seeps through it to an outfall. Where groundwater is high, a perforated PVC or PE pipe along the base increases the volume carried. Prefabricated HDPE drains with such fabric, coco fiber or rag filters avoid hauling stone aggregate, which is always more expensive.

soil-water-212.title: Refilling aquifers on purpose
soil-water-212.text: In Orange County, California, one facility cleans and injects 100 million gallons of water a day, or 90 billion gallons a year. That is artificial groundwater recharge: recharge engineered by people, routing rainwater or reclaimed water into the subsurface. Managed aquifer recharge methods include modifying streambed channels, bank filtration, water spreading and recharge wells. In India, farmers' over-pumping has depleted groundwater. In 2007 the government funded dug-well recharge projects in 100 districts of seven states. Cities face a related task. Stormwater pollution collects in {{ref:soil-water-090}}, and high water tables affect how detention ponds, retention ponds and rain gardens should be designed.

soil-env-129.title: Permafrost, ground frozen for ages
soil-env-129.text: The oldest permafrost has stayed frozen for around 700,000 years. Permafrost is soil, rock or underwater sediment that stays continuously below 0 °C for two years or more. In practice it occurs where the mean annual temperature is 0 °C or below. It underlies about 11% of the global land surface, around 18 million km2. That includes much of Alaska, Canada, Greenland and Siberia, and high mountains such as the Tibetan Plateau. Its thickness ranges from less than a meter to more than 1,500 m. On land it usually lies beneath soil that freezes and thaws with the seasons, the {{ref:soil-env-146}}. Over millennia, dead plant and animal remains have built up in it without fully breaking down. That makes tundra soil a store of carbon. Warming now threatens that store. As the frozen ground thaws, the remains begin to break down again, releasing carbon dioxide or methane, which feeds back into climate change. Thaw also weakens the ground itself. Ice-rich soil can suddenly exceed hydraulic saturation and shift or collapse, endangering the buildings and infrastructure on it.

soil-phys-157.title: Mounds, pingos and polygons raised by frost
soil-phys-157.text: Frost heaving builds whole landscapes of mounds, on Earth and on Mars. Frost-heave landforms are raised-ground features arranged in circles, polygons and stripes. In organic soils such as {{ref:soil-class-070}} they are called {{ref:soil-water-266}}; in mineral soils, {{ref:soil-phys-161}}. They appear in alpine regions even near the equator, as such peat mounds on Mount Kenya show. {{ref:soil-env-170}} grow up to 60 meters high over hundreds of years in Arctic permafrost, fed by upwelling groundwater rather than capillary action. Small earth hummocks in seasonally frozen ground go by thúfur in Iceland and pounus in Fennoscandia. In May 2008 the Phoenix lander touched down on polygonal frost-heave ground on Mars and found ice a few centimeters down.

soil-phys-161.title: Lithalsas, stony mounds lifted by ice
soil-phys-161.text: On the Svalbard archipelago, stony mounds have been heaved up out of the ground. They are lithalsas: frost-raised mounds in permafrost areas with mineral-rich soils, where a perennial ice lens, one that lasts year after year, has grown within the soil. A lithalsa is the mineral-soil counterpart of {{ref:soil-water-266}} among the frost-heave landforms. The term is sometimes also used for those peat mounds and for {{ref:soil-env-170}}.

soil-chem-072.title: Chelated fertilizers keep micronutrient metals in solution
soil-chem-072.text: The phosphate salts in most fertilizers turn trace metal ions into insoluble solids of no use to plants. Chelated fertilizers avoid that trap by supplying manganese, iron, zinc and copper as metal chelates. EDTA is the typical chelating agent, and iron is often given as EDTA or EDDHA chelates. Sprayed on leaves, a chelated nutrient is absorbed and moved better, and less is lost to soil and groundwater. Use of EDTA and NTA is falling 6% a year over toxicity concerns, as greener EDDS and citrate gain ground.

soil-chem-057.title: Thomas Way and the discovery of cation exchange
soil-chem-057.text: The finding that soils swap cations came from Rothamsted Experimental Station in the 19th century. There, Thomas Way and the man profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-074}} showed that soils exchange cations. Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society in England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions. He is considered the father of soil chemistry. William Albrecht is sometimes credited with the discovery. He may only have been the first to link cation exchange with colloidal clay particles.

soil-chem-130.title: Biofilters: letting microbes eat the pollution
