soil-chem-130.text: Engineers have hired microbes to clean water since 1893, when England introduced the trickling filter for wastewater. A biofilter is a bioreactor holding living material that captures pollutants and breaks them down biologically. Microorganisms attach to a bed of sand, crushed rock or gravel and grow into a thin living film that degrades the pollutants. Biofilters treat wastewater, catch harmful chemicals or silt washed off the land, and oxidize air pollutants. {{ref:soil-water-092}}, wetlands and {{ref:soil-water-263}} work the same way. One drawback: buildup of biomass can clog the bed.

soil-chem-030.title: Acid sulfate soils, harmless until they meet air
soil-chem-030.text: Left undisturbed below the water table, acid sulfate soils are benign. Drain them, dig them up or expose them to air, and their sulfides react with oxygen to form sulfuric acid. These are soils, sediments or organic substrates such as {{ref:soil-class-070}}, formed under waterlogged conditions, that contain iron sulfide minerals, mainly {{ref:soil-chem-134}}, or their oxidation products. Drained, they can turn extremely acidic, below pH 4. The acid releases iron, aluminium and other metals and metalloids, particularly arsenic. Together these kill vegetation and fish, acidify groundwater and surface water, and degrade concrete and steel structures to the point of failure. The most prone formed within the last 10,000 years. Then the last major sea level rise mixed seawater sulfate with land sediments rich in iron oxides and organic matter. They are widespread around coasts. In Australia, coastal acid sulfate soils cover an estimated 58,000 km2 beneath estuaries and floodplains. Canal, housing and marina works often disturb them, and droughts can expose them too. Some drained 100 years ago still release acid. Potential acid sulfate soils, or cat-clays, are often left uncultivated or planted with rice to keep them wet. The term was coined for the first International Symposium on Acid Sulfate Soils, held in 1972 at Wageningen.

soil-chem-035.title: Calcareous soils, built on chalk and limestone
soil-chem-035.text: Soils formed on limestone or chalk lean alkaline, and the reason is simple chemistry. A calcareous soil is one formed from or containing a high proportion of calcium carbonate, as calcite or aragonite. The carbonate ion is a base, so soils whose parent material contains it are relatively alkaline. They may have a calcic horizon, a layer of secondary carbonates. It holds above 15% {{ref:soil-fert-060}} and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below. {{ref:soil-class-086}} grows on soils rich in calcium carbonate from underlying chalk or limestone. {{ref:soil-class-121}} are common on calcareous parent materials in arid and semi-arid environments, and loess is often calcareous. In such low-acidity soils, earthworms mix decomposed organic matter into the mineral soil below, forming {{ref:soil-bio-096}}.

soil-bio-001.title: The crowded underworld that keeps soil alive
soil-bio-001.text: Soil is home to circa 59% of the world's biodiversity. Soil biology is the study of the activity and ecology of the microbes and animals that live there. Its subject is soil life, also called soil biota or edaphon. That covers every organism that spends a significant part of its life cycle in the soil profile or at the soil-litter interface. The cast runs from bacteria, fungi, protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}} to earthworms and arthropods. It even includes some snakes and burrowing mammals such as gophers, moles and prairie dogs. These organisms break down {{ref:soil-found-045}}, releasing nutrients for plants. In doing so they strongly shape the soil's fertility, plant growth, soil structure and carbon storage. Soil life powers the nutrient cycles. Without it, organic material would pile up as undecayed litter, with no dark, stable residue formed and no nutrients available to plants. Soil life also guards what it gathers: nitrogen and phosphorus held in its bodies are kept from leaching away. Microbial exudates help hold soil structure together, and earthworms mix the soil as they burrow. For all that, soil biology is a relatively new science with much still unknown. The discovery of {{ref:soil-bio-121}} in 1996 showed that basic questions about how elements cycle through soil remained open.

soil-bio-008.title: Five hundred sheep beneath a football pitch
soil-bio-008.text: The organisms living beneath a football pitch are estimated to equal the size of 500 sheep. Soil biodiversity is the relationship between soil and that variety of life, including the aspects of soil that can be managed with it in mind. Soil is chiefly a habitat for microbes such as bacteria and fungi. It also houses tiny animals such as protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, small ones such as microarthropods and potworms, and larger ones such as earthworms, termites and millipedes. Their primary role is to recycle dead organic material from the plant-based food web above ground. In turn, their activity is a primary factor in how soil forms, physically and chemically. The link shows on maps: natural and farm vegetation boundaries closely follow soil boundaries, even at continental and global scales. Microbial exudates are now accepted as the main force that binds soil particles into clumps and shields carbon from further breakdown. Soil health depends on this diversity. Living covers on the soil and carbon-containing amendments improve it. {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, crop diversification, legume intercrops and organic inputs all correlate with more diverse soil life.

soil-bio-063.title: Biomineralization: life that builds with stone
soil-bio-063.text: Every major lineage of living things has members that make minerals. Biomineralization is the process by which organisms produce or retain inorganic minerals, often to harden or stiffen their tissues. Over 60 different minerals have been identified in organisms. Most are silicates, carbonates or phosphates. Algae, diatoms and sponges build with silica, invertebrates with carbonates, and vertebrates with calcium phosphates and carbonates. Calcium phosphate and carbonate salts are the most common. Paired with organic polymers such as collagen and chitin, they give bones and shells their structural support. Microbes work on a geological scale. Bacteria take part in forming copper, iron and gold deposits, and microorganisms can both precipitate metals from solution and catalyze the dissolution of minerals. Soil sits inside a planetary loop. Bicarbonate released by weathering travels through soil to the sea, where it is turned into carbonate minerals for shells and skeletons. That makes biomineralization a store that locks carbon away, and a force in {{ref:soil-fert-140}}. It can even clean up pollution. Microbes that release phosphate precipitate uranium phosphate minerals in contaminated groundwater, so the uranium moves less. The first evidence of biomineralization dates to some 750 million years ago, and organisms have made mineralized skeletons for the past 550 million years.

soil-bio-040.title: The earthworm, which Darwin ranked among history's great movers
soil-bio-040.text: In 1881 Charles Darwin wrote that few other animals had played so important a part in the history of the world. He meant the earthworm, a soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida. The name covers the largest members of the Oligochaeta. Earthworms live mostly in moist, compost-rich soil. They eat the remains of dead plants and animals, along with protozoa, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, bacteria, fungi and algae, and rank among nature's most important eaters of dead matter. Adults range from 10 mm to 3 m long, though the typical common earthworm grows to about 360 mm. A worm moves by waves of muscle contraction, anchored by bristles called setae. It has no special respiratory organs and breathes through its moist skin. Populations depend on soil temperature, moisture, pH, salts, aeration and texture. Most favor neutral to slightly acidic soils, and their activity can shift pH to suit them. As they feed and burrow they aerate and mix the soil, help release nutrients for plants to take up, and bind soil organic matter to soil minerals. That makes them indicators of soil health. Healthy soil holds more of them, and their gut microbes reveal its condition. They are also vulnerable. {{ref:soil-fert-007}} create acidity fatal to worms, and pesticides kill them. At least three species are listed as extinct and many more as endangered.

soil-bio-025.title: The soil food web, a digestive system for the land
soil-bio-025.text: All soil organic matter passes through a living gut of sorts. The soil food web is the community of organisms living all or part of their lives in soil. It is seen as a network of feeding links that passes energy among them. A food chain follows one linear energy pathway; a food web shows all the potential pathways. Plants are the producers. Using sunlight, they make plant material from carbon dioxide and minerals, and their roots exude acids, sugars and enzymes that feed the web underground. Its members range from bacteria, algae, fungi and protozoa to {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and microarthropods, and on to earthworms, insects and small vertebrates. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break dead plant and animal material into simple nutrients. In this way the web processes dead material much as a digestive system processes food. The work reaches beyond the soil. The web keeps manure, plant residues and pesticides out of water, holds nitrogen back from groundwater, fixes nitrogen and helps water soak in. Its members prey on crop pests and feed animals above ground. Once thought simple, soil food webs turned out to have common omnivory and long, complex chains. Those chains still resist drying, freezing and fumigation. Some influence escapes the diagram, though. Litter transformers, mutualists and {{ref:soil-bio-004}} strongly affect their communities in ways food webs do not capture.

soil-bio-039.title: Soil enzymes, the chemical tools of decay
soil-bio-039.text: Microbes face a problem of scale: much of their food comes as large molecules left by dead plants and animals. Soil enzymes solve it. Released mainly by microbes, they break down soil organic matter and free nutrients for plants. Fungi, bacteria and archaea excrete them, and plant roots produce some. They speed the breakdown of compounds such as cellulose, starch and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, which makes them prominent agents in the cycling of carbon and nitrogen. Some work inside cells, some stay attached to cells, and some float free. Enzymes bound to clay and humic particles are protected from rapid breakdown but are less active, a trade-off between protection and activity. Their spread is highly patchy, varying at the millimeter scale with nutrients, microbes and roots, and from single trees to whole catchments. Farming steers them. Some fertilizers include {{ref:soil-fert-085}}, which hold back the enzyme that breaks down that compound so nutrients are released over a longer period. Enzyme activity was higher with manure than with inorganic fertilizer, though other studies found a mix of mineral and organic inputs better still. Enzymes both stabilize and degrade soil structure, and they play a decisive role in keeping soil healthy.

soil-bio-075.title: Geosmin, the earthy molecule noses catch in traces
soil-bio-075.text: People can smell geosmin at just 0.006 to 0.01 micrograms per liter of water. Geosmin is a chemical with a distinct earthy or musty smell, made by bacteria common in soil and water. Its name joins the Greek geō-, 'earth', and osmē, 'smell'. Nancy N. Gerber and Hubert A. Lechevalier coined it in 1965 after isolating it from actinomycete cultures, and Gerber worked out its structure in 1968. It is a secondary metabolite, a by-product rather than a necessity of life, of cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Phormidium and Planktothrix and of actinomycetes, mainly Streptomyces. It gives beetroot its earthy taste and contributes to petrichor. The natural (−) form is about eight times more potent than the other, with a mean threshold of 9.5 ng/L against 78 ng/L. With 2-methylisoborneol it is the main biological cause of muddy tastes in drinking water and farmed fish worldwide. It is nontoxic to humans and breaks down in acid, yet standard water treatment cannot remove it, so suppliers need combined methods such as advanced oxidation. In the soil it carries signals. It attracts {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, which feed on Streptomyces and spread its spores, and it repels the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans.

soil-bio-012.title: Actinomycetes, the bacteria once mistaken for fungi
soil-bio-012.text: The sweet, earthy smell of healthy soil comes from the volatile compounds of actinomycetes. These are soil bacteria of the phylum Actinomycetota, formerly Actinobacteria. They are Gram-positive and rich in guanine and cytosine, and many grow branching, fungus-like threads called mycelia. The order name Actinomycetales recalls that they were long thought to be fungi. Fungi do similar work, but actinomycetes are much smaller and likely fill a different niche. They decompose the remains of dead organisms so plants can take up the nutrients anew. They also help build stable dark soil matter by breaking down cellulose, tough woody compounds and the chitin of arthropods. The phylum is one of the dominant bacterial groups and includes Streptomyces, one of the largest bacterial genera. Streptomyces and its relatives are major contributors to the biological buffering of soils. Some, such as {{ref:soil-bio-200}}, live with plant roots, fixing nitrogen in exchange for some of the plant's sugars. They need plenty of air and a pH between 6.0 and 7.5, but tolerate dry conditions better than most bacteria and fungi. They also stock the medicine cabinet. They yield many antibiotics, among them streptomycin, neomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline, plus farm compounds such as insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and plant growth promoters.

soil-bio-003.title: Seven hundred kilometers of fungal thread in a gram of soil
soil-bio-003.text: A gram of garden soil can hold around one million fungi and around 700 km of fungal threads, called hyphae. Soil fungi are the yeasts, molds and other fungi of the soil. They lack chlorophyll, spread through the soil as a web of threads called mycelium, and feed on dead plant and animal matter. Bacteria may outnumber them in cell counts, but fungi can contribute more biomass and respiration in some soils. As chemo-heterotrophs, they need organic substrates for their carbon. Their mycelium breaks fresh remains down into {{ref:soil-bio-089}} and carbon dioxide. In that work the key fungi are {{ref:soil-bio-125}}, which turn dead matter into mineral forms such as nitrate, ammonium and phosphate that plants can use. Dead matter is colonized by a succession of species: sugar and starch users first, then those able to break down cellulose and tougher woody compounds. Many fungi are parasites that cause plant disease. Others are beneficial partners, such as {{ref:soil-bio-157}}, and fungi also help bind soil into crumbs and feed larger soil organisms. Compared with bacteria, fungi fare relatively well in acidic soils and in dry soils, which hold more of the oxygen they need. Fruiting bodies such as mushrooms release spores that spread by wind, water and fungus-eating animals and can lie dormant for years.

soil-bio-070.title: Microbial inoculants: bottled helpers for crops
soil-bio-070.text: An estimated 836 million USD is spent on microbial inoculants each year. These farm amendments, also called soil inoculants or bioinoculants, use beneficial microbes that live around or inside roots to promote plant health. Many of the microbes form mutually beneficial partnerships with the crop. Besides improving nutrition, they can promote growth by stimulating the plant's hormone production. Bacterial inoculants, called plant growth promoting {{ref:soil-bio-154}}, include nitrogen fixers and phosphate solubilisers. The most commonly applied is Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen inside legume roots, in the growths covered in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are used to supply phosphorus. In one greenhouse with reduced fertilization, these fungi plus root bacteria gave tomato yields at 70% fertility that matched those at 100%. Inoculants can also induce systemic acquired resistance, a whole-plant defense, shown so far against powdery mildew, take-all, leaf spot and root rot. Mixing strains raises nutrient uptake from soil and fertilizer. Several strains together even raise the activity of the nitrogen-fixing enzyme when only one of them fixes nitrogen. Inoculants often change the soil's existing microbial community. Results so far are mixed. Research in 2024 suggests as few as one in nine commercial products are beneficial, and with commercial products root colonization by these fungi was under 10%. Large-scale application is not yet economically viable, so inoculants are not widely used in industrial agriculture.

soil-bio-015.title: The microbial loop: how predators free nutrients for roots
soil-bio-015.text: Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term microbial loop in 1983 for the role of bacteria in marine carbon and nutrient cycles. It names the pathway by which bacteria take up dissolved organic carbon and pass it back up the food web. 'Microbial food web' is now often used instead. In soil, the loop concerns carbon and the nutrients freed when protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}} eat bacteria fed by roots. It runs like this. Roots pushing into new soil prime resting bacteria, which naked amoebae then eat. That frees mineral nitrogen for root hairs to absorb. Predation by amoebae and free-living roundworms raises the rate at which nutrients are released, which in turn stimulates root growth. This loop is Clarholm's hypothesis, and it is hard to verify by experiment. Bacteria-eating protozoa release the nutrients locked in microbial bodies in a form plants can use. A related idea, the microbial carbon pump model, has plants add carbon through {{ref:soil-bio-142}} and litter. Microbes then either respire it to the atmosphere or store it in a stable pool as dead microbial biomass, called necromass. They transform plant carbon outside the cell with enzymes and inside it as their populations grow and die. The balance between pathways that release CO2 and those that build carbon sets how much carbon the soil keeps. Fresh plant carbon can also prime microbes to break down carbon already stored in soil organic matter faster than models expect. Much remains unknown. Most of the soil microbiome has never been cultivated, which leaves its part in carbon cycling uncertain and hampers climate models of carbon flux.

soil-bio-014.title: Protozoa, the soil's single-celled grazers
soil-bio-014.text: Heterotrophic flagellates may occasionally number several million in a gram of soil. They are the smallest of the soil protozoa, single-celled eukaryotes grouped as flagellates, amoebae and ciliates. Most protozoa eat bacteria. Others eat bacteria and fungi, fungi alone, or particles of decayed plant and animal matter. Naked amoebae move through water-filled pores and films. {{ref:soil-bio-195}} shelter in shells against drying out, and they serve as indicators of past climates. Ciliates, the largest, move by many short beating cilia.

soil-bio-069.title: Soil-borne pathogens, the enemies waiting below the crop
soil-bio-069.text: Some of a plant's worst enemies wait in the ground beneath it. A soil-borne pathogen is a disease-causing agent that lives both in soil and in a plant host, and it tends to infect healthy plants grown in that soil. Common examples are Fusarium, Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Phytophthora, Verticillium, Rhizopus, Thielaviopsis and roundworms such as Meloidogyne. Many are fungi, even though other soil fungi are helpful partners of plants. Their propagules are the spores and fragments that spread them. Chemicals released by plants can stir them to germinate in the soil around a seedling's lower stem. They then start the stem rots that cause damping-off, the collapse of young seedlings. Monoculture and chemical fertilization often bring these diseases, along with acidification and degradation that lower productivity. Growers have several defenses. Fallowing disrupts pathogens by removing their hosts for a while. Heating the soil with sunlight, {{ref:soil-agri-034}}, kills or badly weakens many. Disease-suppressive soils inhibit them, and teas brewed from {{ref:soil-fert-028}} suppress them too. Growing roots in substrates instead of soil, as {{ref:soil-fert-167}} does, eliminates soil-borne diseases and pests altogether.

soil-bio-037.title: How a changing planet is changing soil's breath
soil-bio-037.text: Soil breathing shifts with every change people make to air and land. Free air CO2 enrichment (FACE) studies raise CO2 over open plots. Elevated CO2 boosted soil respiration through more roots and microbial activity, by up to 40.6% in sweetgum and poplar forests. Warming may hit hardest in the Arctic. There, thawing permafrost turns aerobic, and its large carbon stores are respired much faster. Rainfall matters too. Dry soils burst into respiration after rain and slow as they dry, so more frequent, intense rain should raise respiration sharply in arid lands. Nitrogen fertilization since the era covered in {{ref:soil-agri-138}} has boosted plant growth, root respiration and root biomass, and soil respiration along with them.

soil-bio-028.title: Bottom-up control: feed the base and the web swells
soil-bio-028.text: Feed the base of a food web and the whole web grows. In bottom-up control, the biomass, abundance or diversity of higher levels depends on resources from lower levels. The evidence is correlation: consumers rise and fall with their resources. On land, the biomass of herbivores and detritivores rises with primary productivity, the rate at which plants make new growth. In the {{ref:soil-bio-025}} the chain is easy to follow. More productivity means more leaf litter, then more bacteria and fungi, more {{ref:soil-bio-193}} that eat them, and more mites and predatory roundworms. The whole web swells.

soil-bio-031.title: Funnels, cores and lamps: getting animals out of soil
soil-bio-031.text: Counting soil animals starts with getting them out of the soil. Samples are often taken with a metal core. Large animals such as earthworms can be picked out by hand, but that is impossible for {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and small arthropods. A dry Berlese funnel drives microarthropods downward, away from light and heat, into a collecting vial. A wet Baermann funnel collects these worms, which sink because they cannot swim. Microbes need other tricks. They are characterized by their respiration, by genetic profiling of extracted cell components, or by biomass estimated before and after fumigation.

soil-bio-029.title: Do soil predators rule the web from the top?
soil-bio-029.text: Do the hunters in soil control the hunted? In top-down control, consumers higher in a food web set the abundance, diversity or biomass of the levels below. Its signature is the trophic cascade, in which predators affect organisms at least two links down. Whether cascades matter on land is actively debated. In soil they occur in the bacterial and fungal channels, but they may be infrequent. Omnivory, dormancy and the spatial separation of predator and prey all damp top-down effects. Soil webs are also donor controlled: decomposers cannot change how fast litter falls. Added predators or parasites can still matter. A roundworm that kills insects, {{ref:soil-bio-083}}, killed root-eating ghost moth caterpillars and so protected bush lupine. That is the principle behind biological control.

soil-bio-021.title: Soil microfauna, the animals that live in water films
soil-bio-021.text: A tardigrade dried out in soil can wait as a shrunken tun and revive within a few hours. Tardigrades belong to the soil microfauna, the smallest soil animals at 20 μm to 200 μm. The group includes protozoa, {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and rotifers. They move through mesopores (30–75 μm) and macropores (>75 μm) and mostly live in the water films around aggregates and roots. There they eat microbes or one another. Their grazing rejuvenates microbial colonies, and they excrete nutrients such as ammonium in a form plants can use. Tied to pore water, they are sensitive to drying. Cysts, dauer larvae and tuns are their survival stages. Unlike most soil invertebrates, they may not suffer critically from climate warming, but they are highly sensitive to acid rain.

soil-bio-062.title: How plants thrive on the poorest soils
soil-bio-062.text: Plants on nutrient-poor soils get by in three ways: they take up nutrients more efficiently, use less of them and store them. Root adaptations improve uptake, among them nitrogen-fixing {{ref:soil-bio-179}}, fungal partners and {{ref:soil-bio-191}}. These plants grow very slowly. They use abundant ions to keep their cells firm and save scarce nutrients for building tissue. Many store nutrients, in trunk tissue for example, and remobilize them when demand rises. On the ancient sandplains of southern Western Australia, most plants rely on these roots for phosphorus and sulfur. Yet the vegetation is highly diverse. The white-sand soils of the Rio Negro basin in northern Amazonia, with pH below 5.0, tell another story. They carry low-diversity, extremely fragile forests and savannahs.

soil-bio-080.title: Extracellular polymeric substances, the glue of microbial life
soil-bio-080.text: Between 50% and 90% of the organic material in a biofilm is the slime its microbes secrete. Extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) are high-molecular-weight natural polymers that microorganisms release into their surroundings. They are mostly polysaccharides and proteins, with DNA, lipids and humic compounds. They hold biofilms together and protect the microbes inside from harsh conditions, mechanical removal and antimicrobials. Exopolysaccharides help nitrogen-fixing bacteria attach to plant roots and soil particles, so the bacteria can colonize roots and the soil around them. EPS also shape the soil itself. Together with microbial cells they can block soil pores in bioclogging, lowering hydraulic conductivity. They make sediment more stable by changing its cohesion, permeability and erosion, and they affect the precipitation of minerals, especially carbonates. They adsorb metal cations such as copper, lead, nickel and cadmium, which helps clean up heavy metals. EPS from the bacterium Zoogloea and the fungus Aspergillus niger even remove {{ref:soil-env-199}} from contaminated soils, using enzymes that degrade them.

soil-bio-137.title: Roots that breathe, pull, prop and store
soil-bio-137.text: Not every root just anchors and drinks. Specialized roots take on other tasks; they include aerial, prop, buttress, storage and contractile roots, and the tufts described in {{ref:soil-bio-191}}. Those tufts of short rootlets form when phosphate or iron runs low, notably in the Proteaceae. Mangroves raise aerating roots, or {{ref:soil-bio-199}}, above ground or water to exchange gases where soil oxygen is limited. Contractile roots expand sideways and shorten lengthwise, pulling bulbs, corms and some taproots deeper. Swellings in virtually all legumes, described in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}, house nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Coralloid roots near the surface house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

soil-bio-143.title: The rhizosphere, the crowded zone around every root
soil-bio-143.text: Each gram of soil in and around roots can hold up to 10 billion bacterial cells that grow in culture. In 1904 a German plant physiologist, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-075}}, named this crowded zone the rhizosphere. He meant soil around roots whose microbes are partly controlled by chemicals the roots release. Today it is defined as the narrow zone of soil directly influenced by root secretions and by the microorganisms living with the roots. The roots pay generously for their company. They may exude 20–40% of the carbon they fix by photosynthesis as sugars and organic acids. Microbes in the zone's pores feed on these root exudates and on sloughed-off root cells, a process described in {{ref:soil-bio-148}}. The result is a hotspot of microbial diversity. Much of the nutrient cycling plants need happens right beside roots, and so does disease suppression by microbial antibiotics. Organic acids and sugars affect how microbes shuttle phosphorus, nitrogen, potassium and water to the root, and how much iron is available. Root respiration and exudation can create pockets without oxygen next to roots. In acid soils, the pH rises close to roots. At the very center lies the rhizoplane: the root surface itself, with the soil particles closely bound to it.

soil-bio-159.title: Inside the cell or around it: the kinds of mycorrhiza
soil-bio-159.text: The first question about any mycorrhiza is how far the fungus gets into the root. Mycorrhizal types group these partnerships by how the fungus colonizes the root. The main split runs between {{ref:soil-bio-173}} and endomycorrhizas. In the first kind, the hyphae never enter individual root cells. In endomycorrhizas they pass through the cell wall, up to the cell membrane. The endomycorrhizas include the types described in {{ref:soil-bio-166}}, {{ref:soil-bio-176}} and {{ref:soil-bio-186}}, along with arbutoid and monotropoid forms. The lifestyle evolved independently many times. The fungi of the first of those endomycorrhizal types form a single phylum, while other mycorrhizal fungi converged on similar ways of life. Not every fungus inside a root is a partner of this kind. Fungal {{ref:soil-bio-202}} live harmlessly inside plants but lack the structures mycorrhizal fungi use to bring in nutrients from outside. Mucoromycotina fungi of this kind in fine roots were long mistaken for partners of the first type. They seem able to live without a host and prefer wet, acidic soils. In monotropoid mycorrhizas, found in Monotropoideae and some orchids, the flow runs backward. The plant takes its carbon from the fungus, making the association parasitic.

soil-bio-158.title: Sugar for minerals: how the mycorrhizal trade works
soil-bio-158.text: Most mycorrhizal hyphae are far finer than the smallest root or root hair. That fineness is the fungus's whole advantage. Mycorrhizal nutrient exchange is the trade in which the fungus gets carbohydrates from its host and in return improves the plant's uptake of water and minerals. Sugars such as glucose and sucrose travel from their source, usually the leaves, down to the roots and on to the fungus. In exchange, the hyphae explore soil that roots cannot reach and add absorbing surface. They may secrete organic acids that dissolve or chelate ions, or free ions from minerals by ion exchange. They reach phosphate and iron that roots alone cannot, including nutrients immobilized in clay-rich or strongly basic soils. Some mycorrhizal fungi decay organic matter directly. In some nutrient-poor forests their hyphae take phosphate straight from leaf litter, bypassing the soil. Farmers can lean on the trade. {{ref:soil-agri-134}} with Inga, proposed as an alternative to slash-and-burn, relies on the fungi in Inga roots to stop rain washing phosphorus out of the soil. The trade helps most in nutrient-poor soils. Yet in boreal forests the fungi have been found hoarding nitrogen in times of scarcity, so the deal may be more than simply mutualistic.

soil-bio-179.title: Root nodules, the pink factories of fixed nitrogen
soil-bio-179.text: Cut open a working nodule and its fixing zone is pink, colored by leghemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that manages oxygen. A root nodule is a growth on the roots of some plants, chiefly legumes, that houses nitrogen-fixing bacteria: rhizobia in legumes, or {{ref:soil-bio-200}} in other plants. Fixation is very sensitive to oxygen. Nodules form when soil nitrogen is scarce; plenty of it blocks them. Legume roots release flavonoids that attract rhizobia and switch on {{ref:soil-bio-201}}. These make root hairs curl, and an infection thread carries the bacteria into the cortex. Leaf sugars pay for splitting N2. Determinate nodules, as on soybean, stop dividing early and are round. Indeterminate ones, as on pea, alfalfa and clover, keep a growing tip and are cylindrical. Heat, acidic soils, drought and nitrate limit it. When the plant dies, its fixed nitrogen fertilizes the soil, which is why traditional rotations include a legume such as clover.

soil-bio-145.title: The chemical conversation around roots
soil-bio-145.text: Roots send chemical messages, and the soil around them is full of listeners. Rhizosphere signalling is the exchange of chemical signals among roots, microbes, fungi and insects, which decides who colonizes the root zone. Hundreds of root metabolites recruit microbes, letting plants favor helpful bacteria. Rhizobia detect flavonoids from legume roots and reply with {{ref:soil-bio-201}} that lead to root nodules, and each signal pair is strictly specific. Root signals described in {{ref:soil-bio-172}} make mycorrhizal spores germinate and colonize the root. There are eavesdroppers. The parasitic plant Striga germinates when it detects the same signals.

soil-bio-180.title: Actinorhizal plants, the nitrogen fixers that are not legumes
soil-bio-180.text: Some alders fix as much as 300 kg of N2 per hectare per year, close to the highest legume rates. They do it with {{ref:soil-bio-200}}, a nitrogen-fixing actinomycete living in nodules on their roots, and plants with this partnership are called actinorhizal. Apart from the herbaceous Datisca, they are trees or shrubs, in three orders, eight families and twenty-six genera, such as alder, sea-buckthorn and Casuarina. Their nodules let them pioneer nitrogen-poor ground such as moraines, volcanic flows and sand dunes, enriching the soil for later species. Altogether these plants fix roughly as much nitrogen as rhizobial partnerships.

soil-bio-174.title: Fungi that let trees endure poisoned ground
soil-bio-174.text: Some fungi thrive where metals poison most life. Ectomycorrhizal fungi can survive, and help their hosts survive, soils high in heavy metals, salts, radionuclides and organic pollutants. They limit heavy-metal uptake by binding metals at the cell wall and locking them inside cells in complexes, metallothioneins or vacuoles. They can also concentrate metals in their fruiting bodies. Suillus luteus and S. bovinus have forms adapted to zinc, cadmium and copper. Tolerance seems widespread, yet contaminated sites have less diverse fungal communities, while naturally metal-rich soils such as those covered in {{ref:soil-class-060}} do not. Some species help hosts survive salty soil, some break down persistent pollutants such as PCBs, and many hyperaccumulate radionuclides.

soil-bio-155.title: Growth-promoting bacteria, from seed coat to root
soil-bio-155.text: Joseph W. Kloepper first used the term plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, or PGPR, in the late 1970s. They are soil bacteria that colonize plant roots after being inoculated onto seed, and they enhance plant growth. Directly, they fix nitrogen, make siderophores that chelate iron for the root, solubilize minerals such as phosphorus and make plant hormones. Indirectly, they limit the damage pathogens do to yield, through induced systemic resistance and antifungal compounds. To work they must survive on the seed, multiply in the spermosphere, attach to the root and colonize the root system. Failure to colonize often explains poor field results. Inoculants usually go on the seed coat so that enough bacteria establish, and those at the root tip were found most active. Most are Pseudomonadota and Bacillota, such as Pseudomonas putida and Azospirillum lipoferum. As {{ref:soil-fert-048}} and biopesticides, they could raise yields and cut disease while reducing dependence on chemical fertilizers and pesticides.

soil-bio-090.title: Humification, how part of the litter becomes humus
soil-bio-090.text: Not all decaying matter vanishes into carbon dioxide. In humification, soil organisms feeding on litter turn part of it into humus instead of mineralizing it completely. The raw materials are plant detritus, dead animals and microbes, called necromass, the excreta of all soil organisms and black carbon from past fires. Fungi and bacteria that feed on dead matter do the work, along with earthworms, nematodes, protozoa and arthropods. Earthworms are major contributors. The ingredients disappear in order. Sugars, starches, simple proteins and organic acids go first and fast. Cellulose and {{ref:soil-bio-116}} follow more slowly, and fats, waxes and resins persist longest. {{ref:soil-bio-129}} transform that tough polymer quickly, making it a main precursor of humus. Resistant leftovers, such as modified {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, oils, fats and waxes, join newly made compounds like polysaccharides to form the basis of humus. Reactions with proteins lock nitrogen and other nutrients inside, protecting them from mineralization. Early work pictured humification as building polymers that microbes could not attack. Recent research shows microbes can digest humic substances in redox reactions. Humification happens naturally in soil and artificially in {{ref:soil-fert-029}}, and it can darken soils, a change called melanization. For storing carbon long term, stimulating it beats slowing litter decay. Not everyone accepts the idea, though. Some authors reject humification as a distinct process, arguing that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing compounds.

soil-bio-128.title: Dissolved organic matter, soil's most mobile carbon
soil-bio-128.text: Some of the carbon in soil travels with the water. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is the fraction that passes a filter with pores of about 0.22 to 0.7 micrometers; its carbon is dissolved organic carbon (DOC). In soil it comes from rain, litter, crop residues, manure, root exudates and decaying organic matter. It is one of the most active and mobile stores of carbon, affecting soil charge, acid-base reactions, nutrient retention and the trapping of heavy metals. Clays and iron and aluminum oxides hold it. Leached DOC can reach the water table in well-drained soils, and under mor it moves from the E to the B horizon.

soil-class-021.title: The FAO map legend that became a world system
soil-class-021.text: The first truly international soil classification began life as the key to a map. The FAO soil classification, developed by the Food and Agriculture Organization, is a supra-national system that generalizes how soils form from the interaction of the main soil-forming factors. It started as the legend of the FAO–UNESCO map of the world's soils, published from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million. Rudi Dudal led the 1974 legend. It gathered ideas from national systems, among them the diagnostic horizons of the USDA's 1960 '7th approximation'. Its 106 soil units were mapped as associations named for the dominant unit, with soil phases, three texture classes and three slope classes. Simple and broad, it fitted most soils from field descriptions alone. It was meant for continental maps, not local ones. The 1988 Revised Legend had 153 soil units in 28 major soil groupings, and it still underlies the Harmonized World Soil Database. United Nations projects applied the system, and many countries adapted it. Many of its names are known widely, with similar meanings. In the 1974 legend, thin soils on calcareous rock were called {{ref:soil-class-050}} and those on acid rock were called {{ref:soil-class-040}}. The WRB replaced it in 1998.

soil-class-028.title: Gleysolic soils: gray ground where water lingers
soil-class-028.text: Flood a soil warmer than about 5 °C, and microbes use up its oxygen within days. Nitrate and ferric oxide are then reduced, and losing ferric oxide turns the soil gray. When it dries, reoxidized iron forms yellow-brown mottles. Poor drainage and a drab gray color therefore identify the Gleysolic order: Canadian soils periodically or permanently saturated with water and depleted of oxygen. They cover about 117,000 square kilometers, 1.3% of Canada, in depressions and level areas of subhumid and humid climates. Three great groups are defined: the Humic group, with a dark organic A horizon; a plain group, without one; and the Luvic group, with a clay-enriched B horizon.

soil-class-027.title: Podzolic soils under Canada's conifers
soil-class-027.text: Organic acids from forest litter can free iron and aluminum and carry them down through a soil. The result is the Podzolic order: acid soils whose B horizon accumulates amorphous humified organic matter bound to aluminum and iron. These soils form mostly in sandy materials under forest or shrubs in cold, humid climates. Percolating water leaches bases. The metal–organic complexes become insoluble and settle in the B horizon once the metals reach a critical proportion. Podzolic soils occupy 14.3% of Canada, in the Appalachian Uplands, the Canadian Shield and British Columbia, usually under coniferous forest. Great groups follow the B horizon. The Humic group is low in iron, the Ferro-Humic group holds at least 5% organic carbon, and the Humo-Ferric group, the commonest, holds less than 5%.

soil-class-031.title: Luvisolic soils, where clay moves down under forest
soil-class-031.text: Under forest, clay can leave one layer of a soil and settle in the next. The Luvisolic order holds Canadian soils with a leached Ae horizon above a Bt horizon, where the washed-down clay has been deposited. They typically form under forest, in subhumid to humid climates where the parent material holds appreciable clay. In saline or calcareous material, salts and carbonates leach out before the clay moves. Luvisolic soils cover about 809,000 square kilometers, 8.8% of Canada, largely in the central to northern Interior Plains. Two great groups split by soil temperature. The Gray Brown group, at 8 °C or more, lies in the Great Lakes–St Lawrence Lowlands; the Gray group belongs to the boreal Interior Plains.

soil-class-098.title: Histosols, soils built from organic matter
soil-class-098.text: Leave a waterlogged soil alone long enough and it can turn into coal. A Histosol is a soil made primarily of organic materials, recognized by both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy. It has 40 cm or more of organic soil material starting within 40 cm of the surface. Organic material means at least 12% organic carbon in Soil Taxonomy, or 20% in the WRB. Histosols form wherever organic matter accumulates faster than it is destroyed. Usually poor drainage is the cause, because it prevents aerobic decay. Their materials grade from muck to {{ref:soil-class-070}}. Soil Taxonomy's suborders Saprists, Hemists and Fibrists follow those materials, alongside drier Folists and submerged Wassists. With {{ref:soil-class-096}}, Histosols store large quantities of organic carbon, which makes them ecologically very important. They have very low bulk density, and many are acidic and short of major nutrients. Rain-fed {{ref:soil-water-122}}, cut off from groundwater, are especially poor. Histosols are hard to cultivate. Drained ones on young glacial land can make good dairy or beef pasture. But dried organic matter can blow away as powder, and heavy structures subside. Most lie in Canada, Scandinavia, the West Siberian Plain, Sumatra, Borneo and New Guinea, and they cover 1.2% of the world's ice-free land. Australia calls them Organosols. As fossils they appear with the first extensive land vegetation, in the Devonian.

soil-class-080.title: Frozen peat and the carbon it guards
soil-class-080.text: Around half the area of northern peat bogs is frozen year-round. This peatland permafrost covers about a tenth of all permafrost area and holds about a tenth of permafrost carbon, 185 ± 66 Gt. Dry peat insulates well, with a thermal conductivity of around 0.25 W m−1 K−1. It shields the frozen ground from thaw, forming raised features called {{ref:soil-water-266}} and peat plateaus. Thaw tends to raise methane emissions while only slightly increasing CO2 uptake, so it adds to the warming feedback from thawing permafrost carbon. Under 2 °C of global warming, 0.7 million km² of peatland permafrost could thaw.

soil-class-079.title: Rewetting a peatland back to life
soil-class-079.text: A drained bog can often be healed by blocking its ditches. Peatland restoration repairs damaged peat bogs, usually by blocking drainage channels so they rewet and native vegetation recovers. Rewetting limits carbon release in the short term. Later, the new vegetation supplies the litter that restarts peat formation. Actively reintroducing bog plants re-establishes typical communities within 5 years, helping animals, insects and birds return. Pools add microhabitats and raise the variety of life. The Convention on Biological Diversity names peat areas as key ecosystems to protect, and wet habitats in general are also protected under the 1971 treaty covered in {{ref:soil-water-262}}.

soil-class-078.title: Gardening without peat
soil-class-078.text: Peat has long filled garden pots, but that is changing. Peat in horticulture means its use as a raw material for gardening, now restricted in some places. In 1999 the UK set its horticulture industry a target of 90% peat-free by 2010. Kew Gardens has discouraged peat as a soil additive since 2003, and the Royal Horticultural Society promotes peat-free gardening. Peat-free mixes based on bark and {{ref:soil-agri-139}} are rising in the UK, while other European countries, Canada and parts of the US still use peat. Chile has forbidden peat extraction since April 2024. Peat grow cups have about 4.5 times the carbon footprint of single-use plastic cups.

soil-fert-182.title: Liebig's law: the scarcest nutrient sets the limit
soil-fert-182.text: Farmers who added more of a plentiful nutrient saw no gain in growth, while adding the scarce one worked. Explaining that puzzle gave agriculture one of its best-known rules. Liebig's law of the minimum holds that growth is set not by the total resources available but by the scarcest one, the limiting factor. It was developed in agricultural science in 1840 by the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-072}}, and the chemist Liebig later popularized it. In soil terms, when one nutrient is short in the soil solution, stoichiometry keeps the plant from taking up the others at an optimal rate. Stoichiometry means the fixed proportions in which elements are combined. The law spread well beyond the farm. It has been extended to biological populations, and ecosystem models commonly use it for factors such as sunlight, nitrate or phosphate. In the sea, phytoplankton can be limited by iron in nutrient-rich coastal upwellings and by nitrogen and phosphorus in the nutrient-poor open ocean. In natural resource management it implies that growth is restricted by the scarcest input. Phosphorus has no substitute, so it will have to be recycled. The law is not the last word, though. Diagnosing limiting factors is still a common study, but the approach has been criticized. In plant nutrition, models that allow for interactions between nutrients have replaced it.

soil-fert-100.title: Nitrogen fixation: cracking the air's toughest bond
soil-fert-100.text: Two nitrogen atoms in the air cling together with a triple bond so strong that most organisms cannot break it. Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of this abundant but unreactive gas into usable compounds such as ammonia and nitrate. Life depends on it, because DNA, proteins and other vital organic compounds all contain nitrogen. It is the gateway into {{ref:soil-fert-099}}, and it happens in three ways. Lightning does it naturally, making nitrogen oxides that form nitrous and nitric acids. These seep into soil as nitrate that plants can use. Industry does it artificially. About 30% of all fixed nitrogen is now made by the method in {{ref:soil-fert-104}}. Living things do the rest. Lightning fixes 5 to 10 billion kg a year, but free-living or symbiotic bacteria do most of the work. They are the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-102}}. Their tools are enzymes, described in {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, made by microorganisms such as cyanobacteria and rhizobia. Some of these microbes live in partnership with legumes, mosses and the water fern covered in {{ref:soil-fert-204}}. Looser associations also occur, for example on rice roots.

soil-fert-105.title: How bacteria were caught pulling nitrogen from the air
soil-fert-105.text: In 1838 the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-073}} discovered biological nitrogen fixation. Explaining it took the rest of the century. Experiments in 1855 and 1887 had shown that nitrogen did not enter plants directly from the air. Between 1886 and 1888, Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth found the role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria, opening a new era of soil science. Some sources date their discovery to 1880 or 1887. In 1901 Beijerinck showed that Azotobacter chroococcum fixes atmospheric nitrogen. It was the first known free-living fixer of its kind, the group covered in {{ref:soil-fert-102}}.

soil-fert-102.title: Diazotrophs, the microbes that live on air
soil-fert-102.text: A small water fern in rice paddies carries its own nitrogen supply. {{ref:soil-fert-204}} harbours the cyanobacterium Anabaena, and farmers value it as a living nitrogen source for rice, the practice covered in {{ref:soil-fert-026}}. Anabaena is a diazotroph: an organism, usually a bacterium or archaeon, that can fix atmospheric nitrogen gas into usable compounds such as ammonia. Diazotrophs are scattered across many groups of bacteria and a few archaea, including rhizobia, Frankia and Azospirillum. Symbiotic diazotrophs were long thought to matter more globally, but free-living ones are also significant fixers. Obligate anaerobes such as Clostridium live in low-oxygen soils and decaying plant matter, and methanogenic archaea fix nitrogen in oxygen-poor soils. Fixation costs so much energy that diazotrophs cut it back when other nitrogen is available and, in many species, when oxygen is high. Aerobic fixers such as Azotobacter vinelandii shield their fixing enzymes, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, with very high respiration rates and protective compounds. On land, diazotrophs supply the nitrogen that primary producers use, and that fixed nitrogen can reduce the need for fertilizer.
